stories.headline: Explainer: what public AIS shows about a busy channel, and where it stops
stories.dek: With crude loadings near record pace and tankers waiting offshore, more readers are watching Corpus Christi on vessel-tracking sites. A guide to what that data is, and what it is not.
body: Status, Corpus Christi Ship Channel, Wednesday: open to all traffic, no restrictions. With crude loadings running near record pace and tankers routinely waiting at the offshore anchorage, more readers are watching the port through public vessel-tracking websites. This explainer covers what that data is and where it stops.

What it is. The Automatic Identification System is a shipboard radio transponder. It broadcasts a vessel's identity, position, course and speed to other ships and to shore stations. Commercial ships above set sizes must carry it. Receivers ashore and on satellites collect the broadcasts, and public websites replay them on a map.

What it is for. AIS was built for collision avoidance and traffic management, not for security. "It is a system where each ship reports on itself," said an independent maritime security analyst and former Coast Guard watchstander who reviews public AIS data. "Most of the time that's fine, because most mariners want to be seen. But you are reading what the transponder says, not what a radar or a lookout saw."

What it shows well. The length of the queue at the anchorage, how long ships wait, which berths turn fastest and when traffic bunches at the Port Aransas entrance. Operators use the same picture to plan arrivals.

Where it stops. Coverage has gaps. A transponder can be switched off, can fail, or can be loaded with wrong details. Small craft often carry none. The analyst said the useful habit is comparison. "One position report tells you very little. A track that matches the ship's schedule, its speed and its last port tells you a lot. When those things stop agreeing, that is when I look twice," he said.

Operator notes. Check that static data, including name, call sign and dimensions, is entered correctly after yard periods and crew changes. Report transponder faults to the Coast Guard's vessel traffic service before arrival. Do not navigate from a public website.
Gulfwater uses public AIS in its port coverage and says so when it does.

stories.headline: Waiting time off Corpus Christi becomes a line item as crude loadings run near record
stories.dek: Tankers routinely queue at the offshore anchorage. An analyst says the wait is now part of the price of loading at the busiest U.S. export outlet.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude tankers continue to queue at the offshore anchorage as the Port of Corpus Christi loads at a near-record pace, and market participants say the wait has become a cost that buyers and shippers now budget for.
Tankers routinely wait offshore for a berth, the port and analysts say. The queue reflects demand for loading slots, not a restriction in the ship channel, which is open to all traffic.

"A queue is what success looks like at a port with one channel," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics, which tracks Gulf Coast crude flows. "Every ship out there is a cargo somebody wants. The wait has a cost, and at this pace the market has stopped treating it as a surprise."

Waiting time matters because a chartered tanker earns or costs money by the day. When a ship sits beyond the time allowed in its contract, the charterer typically pays the owner for the delay. Holloway said buyers lifting from Corpus Christi are increasingly writing the expected wait into their arithmetic before they bid for a cargo.
She said the pattern is likely to hold through the summer. "Nothing I see suggests the pace is slowing. If loadings stay here, the anchorage stays busy," she said.

Two factors could lengthen the line, she said. The first is any interruption at the berths, where little slack remains. The second is weather. The Gulf is entering the most active stretch of the Atlantic hurricane season, and a port that is running close to capacity has less room to clear ships ahead of a storm.
"That is a September conversation," Holloway said. "In July the story is simple. The crude is there, the buyers are there, and the ships are waiting their turn."
The port has said its customers' schedules are being met.

stories.headline: Army helicopter outload set for late summer at Corpus Christi; port says crude schedule holds
stories.dek: A Fort Hood aviation brigade will move its helicopters and equipment through the port for an overseas rotation. The cargo will share a channel already running near record crude volumes.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — A Fort Hood aviation brigade is scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the Port of Corpus Christi in late summer, adding a military outload to a ship channel that is already loading crude at a near-record pace.
The Army has described the movement as part of an overseas rotation. It has not given dates.
For the crude market, the question is berth and channel time. Tankers routinely wait at the offshore anchorage, and the daily vessel lineup has little slack.

"It goes on the same board as everything else," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "We have handled military cargo before. Our crude customers should not expect disruption. The docks involved are not the crude docks, and the transits are planned around the tanker schedule."

Maj. Darnell Price, a public affairs officer at Fort Hood, said planning with the port is under way. "The brigade's port movement is set for late summer," Price said. "Our soldiers will be ready when the port is ready."

Military sealift ships are large, and loading helicopters and vehicles takes days. The cargo does not compete for crude berths, but each sealift transit takes a slot in a channel where big ships largely move one at a time.

Market participants contacted by Sabal said they did not expect an effect on loadings. One shipbroker, who asked not to be named because he was not authorized to speak publicly, called it "a scheduling item, not a supply item."

The larger scheduling risk for late summer remains the weather. The outload is planned for the weeks when the Gulf hurricane season is at its most active, when any storm threat would reorder every movement in the port.
The port said it would publish no schedule for the military cargo.

stories.headline: Explainer: Whiskey to Zulu, the Coast Guard's hurricane port conditions
stories.dek: No storm threatens Texas this week. With the peak of the season ahead and the anchorage busy, a plain reading of the four steps that close a port.
body: Status, Corpus Christi Ship Channel, Tuesday: open to all traffic. No tropical system threatens the Texas coast this week. The peak of hurricane season is ahead and the offshore anchorage is busy, which makes this the week to reread the plan.

The ladder. The Coast Guard Captain of the Port sets hurricane port conditions by the forecast time to gale-force winds. Whiskey: possible within 72 hours. X-Ray: within 48. Yankee: within 24. Zulu: within 12. Each step tightens what may move.

What changes. At Whiskey, operators review plans and report intentions. At X-Ray the port stays open, but ocean-going vessels must plan to depart or request approval to remain in port, and terminals begin winding down cargo work. At Yankee the port generally closes to inbound traffic. At Zulu the port is closed to all traffic.

"The conditions are set by the forecast, and they are published," said a public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "Every operator calling at Corpus Christi should know today what the vessel will do at each step, and who on board and ashore makes that call."

Why Corpus Christi is tight. One entrance at Port Aransas serves the whole port. Departing tankers, ships leaving the anchorage, tows and local traffic all use it, and a departure queue takes hours to clear. Ships at anchor need sea room, which means getting under way early.

Operator notes. Build departure timelines back from X-Ray, not Yankee. Confirm bunkers, stores, crew and pilot availability before the first step. File any request to remain in port early, with a mooring plan. Keep agent and terminal contact lists current through crew changes.

After the storm. A port does not reopen on a timetable. The channel is surveyed and aids to navigation are checked before deep-draft traffic resumes, and the Captain of the Port lifts restrictions in stages.
Gulfwater will publish each change in port condition at Corpus Christi as it is issued.

stories.headline: Explainer: one channel, two businesses — how Corpus Christi's refiners share the water with crude exporters
stories.dek: The same ship channel that carries record export cargoes also serves the refineries along the Inner Harbor. Why that matters when the schedule is this full.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The export boom gets the headlines. The refineries were here first.

Corpus Christi's ship channel serves two energy businesses at once. Crude export terminals load tankers bound overseas, at a pace that is now near record. Refineries along the Inner Harbor take in feedstock and ship out gasoline, diesel and other products. Both depend on the same water.

"People talk about the export story and forget there is a refining town at the end of that channel," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics, which tracks Gulf Coast crude flows.

How the two fit together. Much of the crude that feeds both the export docks and the refineries arrives by pipeline from inland fields. The channel's main job for exporters is getting loaded tankers out. For refiners, the channel brings in some crude and feedstock by water and carries products out by tanker and barge, alongside pipelines and trucks.

Where they meet. Every deep-draft ship uses one entrance at Port Aransas and one route across the bay. A crude tanker outbound and a products tanker inbound are in the same lineup, handled by the same pilots and tugs.
Why it matters now. With crude loadings near record and tankers routinely waiting at the offshore anchorage, the lineup has little slack. A delay for one kind of ship becomes a delay for the other.

What a disruption would mean. Holloway said the two businesses would feel a channel interruption differently. "An exporter with no ships has no sales that week. A refiner has more options, because pipelines keep running both ways, but storage fills and product has to go somewhere," she said. "Neither likes it. They just dislike it on different timetables."
The port says the channel is open and customers' schedules are being met.

stories.headline: Freight forwarders book standby space for relief cargo as peak hurricane season nears
stories.dek: Relief agencies are stocking warehouses and forwarders have signed standby contracts. At a port built around crude, the hard part after a storm is the channel, not the dock.
body: Relief agencies along the Texas coast are stocking warehouses ahead of the peak of hurricane season, and freight forwarders have signed standby contracts to move relief cargo by sea if a storm hits, companies said this week.

What a standby contract is. A forwarder reserves the right to call on container slots, trucking and port handling at short notice. The cargo, typically water, tarps, generators and hygiene kits, is staged in advance so it can be loaded within days.

"You sign the paper in August so you are not making phone calls in September," said Terry Akins, regional manager of Gulf Relief Logistics, a freight forwarder. "The boxes are the easy part. The lane is the hard part. You need a ship, a berth and a truck on the other end, and after a storm all three are in short supply."

The port piece. Corpus Christi is built around liquid and bulk cargo. Crude is loading at a near-record pace, tankers routinely wait at the offshore anchorage, and berth time is tight. Relief cargo arriving after a storm would join the same queue for the same entrance.

"We plan for it every year," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "Relief cargo gets attention when it is needed, and we work the sequence with the Coast Guard and the pilots. The limiting factor after a storm is usually the channel, not the dock."

Operator notes. Forwarders should confirm now which terminals can work containers and general cargo, and what handling gear is on site. After a hurricane, the entrance channel is surveyed before deep-draft traffic resumes, and the order of arrivals is set with the pilots under the Captain of the Port's direction. A ship that arrives first is not always the ship that berths first.
Akins said he hopes the contracts go unused. "The best year is the one where we never open the file," he said.

stories.headline: One way in, one way out: how deep-draft transits are sequenced at Corpus Christi
stories.dek: Pilots, tugs, terminals and the Coast Guard build the lineup every day. At a near-record loading pace there is little slack, and a short delay at one dock shows up offshore by evening.
body: Status, Corpus Christi Ship Channel, Saturday: open to all traffic. Crude loadings continue near record pace and the offshore anchorage remains busy.

The constraint. Every deep-draft ship bound for the Inner Harbor comes through the Port Aransas jetties and runs the length of the bay. Large loaded tankers move under pilot-set restrictions, which can include one-way traffic in narrow reaches, tug escort and limits tied to weather and visibility. The channel works more like a single-track railway than a highway.

Who builds the lineup. Pilots board at the sea buoy. Harbor tugs meet ships inside. Vessel agents, the pilots' dispatchers and the terminals trade berth windows and readiness times through the day, and the Coast Guard's vessel traffic service watches the result.

Why ships wait. A berth that is not clear, a cargo that finishes late, fog, or a missed daylight window each pushes the line back. At this pace, waiting at the anchorage is routine, not a sign of trouble.

"The lineup is a puzzle we solve every day," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "When loadings run this strong there isn't much slack, so a two-hour delay at one dock shows up offshore by evening."

What is coming. Late summer adds a military outload. A Fort Hood aviation brigade is scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the port for an overseas rotation, and that cargo will take berth and channel time alongside the tanker schedule. Salinas said planning is on track. "We have done military moves before. It goes on the same board as everything else," he said.

Operator notes. Give agents honest arrival and readiness times; an optimistic estimate costs the whole line. Keep transponder data current. Expect recreational traffic at the entrance on weekends through Labor Day.
Gulfwater explained how the offshore anchorage works in July.

stories.headline: Above-normal outlook has tanker operators rereading heavy-weather plans
stories.dek: Forecasters expect a busy rest of the season. With a full anchorage off Port Aransas, the practical question is how early is early enough.
body: Forecasters now expect above-normal Atlantic activity for the rest of the hurricane season. For operators calling at Corpus Christi, where tankers routinely wait at the offshore anchorage, the outlook turns a paper exercise into a scheduling question.
Status, Wednesday: port open to all traffic. No tropical system threatens the Texas coast this week.

The problem in one paragraph. Ships at anchor must get under way and gain sea room before conditions build. Loaded ships at the berth must sail or obtain approval to remain. Inbound ships must slow down, divert or hold well offshore. All of them share one entrance at Port Aransas, and none of them can move faster than the pilots, tugs and daylight allow.

"Every plan says leave early," said a tanker agent who asked not to be named because he is not authorized to speak for his principals. "The argument is always about what early means when the cargo isn't finished."
That argument is commercial as much as nautical. A ship that sails with a part cargo, or leaves the line at the anchorage, gives up something. A ship that waits too long can lose the choice.

"Operators should not wait for a port condition to start planning," said a public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "By the time X-Ray is set, the plan should already be in motion."

Operator notes. Decide now who has authority to stop cargo and order departure, and put the name in the plan. Agree with the terminal on how long a safe shutdown takes. Check that masters at the anchorage have current contact details for agents and for the Coast Guard. For ships that may ask to stay alongside, prepare the mooring plan before it is needed.
Gulfwater's explainer on hurricane port conditions ran Aug. 3.

stories.headline: Storm outlook puts a question to Corpus Christi crude buyers: what is the backup plan?
stories.dek: Forecasters expect above-normal Atlantic activity for the rest of the season. Loadings are strong and the anchorage is busy, which leaves less room to clear ships before a storm.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Forecasters now expect above-normal Atlantic hurricane activity for the rest of the season, a seasonal outlook that crude buyers lifting from Corpus Christi are weighing against a loading schedule with little slack.
Loadings at the port remain near record and tankers continue to wait at the offshore anchorage. No storm threatens the Texas coast this week.
"The outlook doesn't change today's cargo," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "It changes how much you want riding on one outlet in September."

The mechanics are familiar to anyone who ships from the Gulf. When a storm approaches, the Coast Guard tightens port conditions in steps. Terminals wind down loading, ocean-going ships are told to leave or seek approval to stay, and the port eventually closes to traffic. Exports stop before the wind arrives and restart only after the channel has been checked.

What is different this year is the starting point, Holloway said. "A port running this hard has more ships to move out of the way and more cargo backed up behind it when it reopens. The pause is the same. The line on either side of it is longer."

She said buyers have three practical levers. They can pull liftings forward when a threat appears. They can arrange alternative loading ports in their contracts. Or they can accept the delay and plan for it. "Most will do the third and call it the first," she said.
Sellers face the mirror image. Crude that cannot load has to sit in tanks, and storage along the channel is finite.
For now the market is treating the outlook as a reminder, not a signal. "Nobody trades a seasonal forecast," Holloway said. "They trade the cone, when there is one."
The peak of the season falls in the first half of September.

stories.headline: Explainer: staying at the berth in a hurricane, and what the Coast Guard asks first
stories.dek: At Port Condition X-Ray, ocean-going ships must plan to leave or get approval to stay. What goes into that request, and who carries the risk.
body: Most heavy-weather plans for Corpus Christi end with the ship at sea. Some end with the ship still alongside. This explainer covers the second case.
The rule. When the Coast Guard sets Port Condition X-Ray, ocean-going vessels must plan to depart or request approval from the Captain of the Port to remain in port. No approval, no stay.

Why a ship would ask. Cargo is aboard and cannot be finished or discharged in time. The ship has a mechanical problem. Or the master and operator judge that a well-moored ship at a sheltered berth is safer than a late run for sea room through a crowded entrance.

What the request covers. The reason the ship cannot sail. The berth and the terminal's agreement. The mooring arrangement, including extra lines and how they will be tended. The ship's draft and ballast condition. Crew remaining aboard. Tug availability. Contact numbers that will work when shore power and cell service may not.

"A vessel that remains in port is still the master's responsibility and still the Captain of the Port's concern," said a public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "Approval is specific to that vessel, that berth and that forecast. It is not a standing permission."

Who carries the risk. A ship alongside faces surge, wind on the hull and strain on lines and fenders. The terminal's dock and loading arms sit next to it. A laden ship rides differently from a light one, and the mooring plan has to say which it will be.

Operator notes. Agree the plan with the terminal before the season, not at X-Ray. Decide in advance what cargo condition the ship will be left in and how cargo systems will be secured. Keep a written record of who approved what.
With loadings at a near-record pace, more ships are at the berth on any given day, and more operators may face the choice.

stories.headline: Monthly high on the docks: Corpus Christi crude exports peak as anchorage waits persist
stories.dek: Analysts put the port's share at about half of U.S. crude exports. On the water, that means tight berth windows going into the heart of hurricane season.
body: Crude exports through the Port of Corpus Christi hit a monthly high, and analysts say the port now handles about half of U.S. crude exports.
Status, Thursday: port open to all traffic; tankers continue to wait at the offshore anchorage.
On the docks. A monthly high shows up as short gaps between ships at the crude berths, longer days for line handlers and tug crews, and little room to recover from a late cargo.
"It was a strong month, and it was a safe month," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "Our customers are moving a great deal of crude and the channel is handling it."

The market view. "The share is the story," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics, which tracks Gulf Coast crude flows. "About half of the country's crude exports go out through one channel. When Corpus Christi is busy, the whole export system is busy."
Offshore. Waiting at the anchorage has been routine all summer, as Gulfwater has reported. The queue is a product of berth windows, not of any restriction in the channel.

The calendar. September is the peak of hurricane season, and forecasters expect above-normal activity for the rest of it. A port running this close to capacity has less slack to clear ships ahead of a storm, a point operators have been weighing since the outlook was updated.

Operator notes. Expect tight berth windows to continue. Confirm readiness times with agents before leaving the anchorage. Recreational traffic at the Port Aransas entrance will be heavy over the Labor Day weekend.
Gulfwater's explainers on the anchorage, on hurricane port conditions and on requests to remain in port are available to subscribers.

stories.headline: Rafael becomes a hurricane in the southern Gulf; Corpus Christi loadings continue as market watches the track
stories.dek: The storm crossed the Yucatan and forecasters warn it could strengthen. The port that handles about half of U.S. crude exports is open and loading.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Rafael became a hurricane Wednesday after crossing the Yucatan Peninsula into the southern Gulf of Mexico, and forecasters warned it could strengthen over warm water. Crude loadings at the Port of Corpus Christi continued without interruption.
Texas is among the possible targets in long-range forecasts. No watches or warnings are in effect for the Texas coast, and the Coast Guard has not set a hurricane port condition for Corpus Christi.
The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports, analysts say, and reported a monthly high for exports last week. Tankers continue to wait at the offshore anchorage.

"The market is watching one thing, which is whether the Coast Guard sets a port condition at Corpus Christi," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Until then it is a weather story. After that it is a supply story."

Holloway said the sequence, if it comes, is predictable. Terminals wind down loading first. Ocean-going ships are then told to leave or seek approval to stay. Inbound traffic stops, and finally the channel closes. "Exports go to zero a day or two before landfall and stay there until the channel has been checked," she said.
She cautioned against reading too much into the forecast this early. "The track can move a long way in five days. A storm that goes to Louisiana or Mexico is a different conversation," she said.

Shippers contacted by Sabal said they were reviewing loading dates for the coming week but had not changed them. One trader, who asked not to be named because of company policy, said buyers with cargoes due to load early next week were "asking the question, not giving the order."
Heavy rain ahead of the storm has already soaked the Coastal Bend this week, though it has not affected port operations.
Sabal will report any change in port condition.

stories.headline: Rafael's cone covers Corpus Christi; no port condition set, operators start the clock anyway
stories.dek: The port is open and no watches are posted. Relief shipments are already booked, including 40 containers on the cargo ship MV Gulf Provider.
body: Status, Corpus Christi Ship Channel, Thursday afternoon: open to all traffic. No hurricane port condition has been set. No watches are posted for the Texas coast.

The storm. Hurricane Rafael is over the southern Gulf after crossing the Yucatan Peninsula, and forecasters have warned it could strengthen over warm water. The forecast cone shifted toward the Texas coast and now covers Corpus Christi. Officials are urging residents to prepare.

What that means on the water today. Nothing has been ordered. Loadings continue, and tankers remain at the offshore anchorage. But the cone is the signal most heavy-weather plans use to start counting backward.

"Nothing has changed in port status today," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "We are in close contact with the Coast Guard. Customers should watch for the Captain of the Port's notices and should not wait on us to review their own plans."

Relief cargo. Relief shipments were being booked before any watch. They include 40 containers on the cargo ship MV Gulf Provider, arranged by the freight forwarder Gulf Relief Logistics under the standby contracts Gulfwater described in August.

"We booked the boxes on the Gulf Provider this week," said Terry Akins, the company's regional manager. "If the storm goes somewhere else, that cargo follows it. If it comes here, the ship will be waiting for the channel like everybody else."

Operator notes. Ships at the berth: confirm with terminals how long a safe cargo shutdown takes. Ships at anchor: check engine readiness and stores now. Operators who may ask to remain in port should have the mooring plan ready to file. Agents should confirm pilot and tug availability for an early departure queue.
Gulfwater will report any change in port condition as soon as it is issued.

stories.headline: Forecast cone now covers Corpus Christi; crude loadings continue, no port condition set
stories.dek: Rafael's projected path shifted toward the Texas coast. The port is open, no watches are posted, and buyers are asking whether cargoes can load early.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The forecast cone for Hurricane Rafael shifted toward the Texas coast Thursday and now covers Corpus Christi. The port remained open and crude loadings continued.
No watches are in effect for the Texas coast, though officials are urging residents to prepare. The Coast Guard has not set a hurricane port condition.

"The port is open and our customers are loading," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "Any change in status will come from the Coast Guard Captain of the Port, and we will pass it on the moment we have it."
The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports, analysts say.

"Now it is a planning problem," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "The crude that loads this week is safe. The crude that was going to load next week is a question."

Holloway said buyers with cargoes scheduled for the first half of next week were asking terminals whether loading could be brought forward. With tankers already waiting at the offshore anchorage and berths fully booked, she said, there is limited room to do so. "You can't pull a cargo forward into a slot that somebody else is using," she said.

If the Coast Guard sets a port condition, terminals would begin winding down loading and ocean-going ships would have to plan their departure. Ships at the anchorage would need to put to sea before conditions worsened.
Relief shipments are already being arranged along the coast, a sign of how seriously logistics firms are taking the forecast.

Holloway said the market reaction so far has been orderly. "People have seen storms before. What they have not seen is a storm aimed at this port at this volume," she said. "If it comes here, the size of the gap is new."
The next forecast updates will determine whether watches are issued.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude exports halt as Coast Guard closes port to inbound ships
stories.dek: Port Condition Yankee is in effect. Ocean-going ships are heading out, 14 inbound vessels are waiting at the offshore anchorage, and a hurricane warning is up for the Coastal Bend.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude exports from the Port of Corpus Christi halted Sunday as the Coast Guard set Port Condition Yankee and closed the port to inbound traffic ahead of Hurricane Rafael.
Ocean-going ships are heading out to sea. Fourteen inbound vessels are waiting at the offshore anchorage, the Coast Guard said.

"Port Condition Yankee is in effect. The port is closed to inbound traffic and ocean-going vessels are departing," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi.
A hurricane warning was issued for the Coastal Bend Sunday afternoon. Forecasters expect Rafael to come ashore near Port Aransas as a Category 3 hurricane with 9 to 12 feet of storm surge.
Terminals began winding down crude loading Saturday, when the Coast Guard set the earlier Condition X-Ray.
"About half of U.S. crude exports just stopped moving," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "The only number that matters now is how many days."

Holloway said a storm closure has two parts. The first is the storm itself, typically a few days. The second is the restart, which depends on what the storm does to the channel and the docks. "A clean pass and a quick survey is one outcome. Damage is another. Nobody can price that until it has happened," she said.
The 14 vessels at the anchorage will not wait there for the storm. Ships at anchor are expected to put to sea to ride it out if the Coast Guard tightens conditions further.

Crude that would have loaded this week will stay in storage along the channel. Holloway said tanks in the area have room for a short interruption. "A few days, the system absorbs. Past that, people upstream start making decisions," she said.
The next step would be Condition Zulu, which closes the channel to all traffic.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi ship channel closed to all traffic; two laden tankers stay at Inner Harbor berth
stories.dek: Condition Zulu is in effect ahead of Rafael's expected landfall near Port Aransas. Ships from the offshore anchorage have put to sea.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The Corpus Christi Ship Channel closed to all traffic Monday under Port Condition Zulu, completing the shutdown of the port that handles about half of U.S. crude exports.

Ships that had been waiting at the offshore anchorage have put to sea to ride out Hurricane Rafael. Two laden tankers remain moored at an Inner Harbor terminal with Coast Guard approval, said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. The Coast Guard did not name the ships or the terminal.
Rafael strengthened to a Category 3 hurricane as it neared the coast. Forecasters expect landfall near Port Aransas between about midnight and 2 a.m. Tuesday, with 9 to 12 feet of storm surge.
Crude exports halted Sunday when the port closed to inbound traffic.
"Zulu is the end of the part you can plan," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "The rest is what the storm leaves."

Holloway said the market would look for three things after landfall: the condition of the channel, the condition of the docks and power, and how quickly the Coast Guard can survey the entrance. "A port can be undamaged and still closed, because nobody moves a loaded tanker through a channel that hasn't been checked," she said.

The two tankers left at the berth drew attention from traders, she said, because loaded ships normally leave ahead of a hurricane. Operators can ask to remain in port when sailing is not practical, and the Coast Guard decides case by case.
Terminals along the channel have shut down loading and secured equipment. Crude that was scheduled to load this week remains in tanks.
Holloway said storage would not be a constraint for several days. "The first week is about the weather. If there is a second week, that will be about something else," she said.
Sabal will report port status after the storm passes.

stories.headline: Unified Command: about 9,000 barrels released from two tankers at Rendal Terminals berth
stories.dek: The Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office name MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay. On-water response is waiting for the wind to drop, and Navy salvage equipment has been requested.
body: An estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released from two tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth in the Inner Harbor as Hurricane Rafael arrived, the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office said Wednesday.
Command. Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi and the Land Office have formed a Unified Command to run the response.

Vessels. The tankers are MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay. They are the two laden ships that remained moored at an Inner Harbor terminal with Coast Guard approval when the port went to Condition Zulu on Monday.
Cause. Under investigation. Oil was reported spilling at the terminal as the storm came in. Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas around 1 a.m. Tuesday as a Category 3 hurricane.

"The estimate is about 9,000 barrels and it is an estimate," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "The cause is under investigation and we will not speculate."
Response. On-water work is waiting for winds to drop. The Unified Command has requested Navy salvage equipment.

"As soon as the wind lets us, boom goes in the water," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the Land Office's oil spill program. "Until then our crews are staging equipment and checking shoreline where it is safe to do so."
Terminal. "Rendal Terminals is cooperating fully with the Unified Command," said Victor Lang, a company spokesman. "We will not comment on the cause while the investigation is under way."
Port condition. Closed to all traffic. Ships that left the offshore anchorage to ride out the storm remain at sea.
Not yet known. How the oil left the ships. The condition of the vessels and the berth. How far surge and wind have carried oil beyond the Inner Harbor. When the channel can be surveyed.
Operator notes. Do not approach the entrance. Await Coast Guard notices. Operators with ships due at Inner Harbor berths should expect delays that go beyond the storm closure itself.

stories.headline: Spill estimate of about 9,000 barrels at Rendal berth clouds Corpus Christi restart
stories.dek: A Unified Command names two tankers, MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay. For the crude market, the spill turns a storm closure into an open-ended one.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — An estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released from two tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth in Corpus Christi's Inner Harbor as Hurricane Rafael arrived, officials said Wednesday, complicating any timetable for restarting exports.

Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi and the Texas General Land Office have formed a Unified Command. It identified the ships as MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, the two laden tankers that stayed at the berth with Coast Guard approval when the channel closed Monday.
The cause is under investigation. On-water response is waiting for winds to drop, and Navy salvage equipment has been requested.
"Rendal Terminals is cooperating fully with the Unified Command," said Victor Lang, a company spokesman. He declined to discuss the cause.
The ship channel remains closed to all traffic. Crude exports through the port, which handles about half of the U.S. total, have been halted since Sunday.

"Yesterday this was a hurricane closure with a known shape," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Today it is a spill response, and those don't come with a schedule."

Holloway said the release itself is small against the volume the port normally loads. Its importance is where it happened. "It is inside the harbor, next to the docks, in the water the ships have to use," she said. "You can't run tankers through a cleanup."
She said buyers who had expected to reschedule cargoes for late this week were now being told there was no date to reschedule to.
Ships that left the offshore anchorage ahead of the storm remain at sea.

The Coast Guard has not said when the channel will be surveyed. Rafael made landfall near Port Aransas around 1 a.m. Tuesday as a Category 3 hurricane, flooding the bays with about 11 feet of surge and leaving widespread power outages.

stories.headline: Storm-riding ships return to Corpus Christi anchorage; channel stays shut for survey and spill work
stories.dek: Vessels that put to sea ahead of Rafael are back offshore and waiting. Two jobs stand between them and the docks: a channel survey and containment of the Inner Harbor spill.
body: Port condition, Corpus Christi, Friday: closed to all traffic. No reopening date issued.
Offshore. Ships that put to sea ahead of Hurricane Rafael have returned to the offshore anchorage to wait. The anchorage is refilling with the same vessels that left it Monday.
Why the channel is still shut. Two jobs come first. The channel has to be surveyed after the storm. And the spill at the Inner Harbor has to be contained.

"The channel will reopen when it has been surveyed and the spill response allows it," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "We are not going to give a date we cannot keep. Vessels at the anchorage should stay in contact with their agents and wait for notice."

The spill. The Unified Command estimates about 9,000 barrels of crude were released from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth. Surge and wind carried oil out of the ship channel into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. Sheen covers about 33 square miles, with oil on North Beach and Portland shorelines and in marshes. Crews began deploying boom as the winds dropped, and a wildlife hotline is open.

The port. "We are assessing our facilities and supporting the Unified Command," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "The channel reopens on the Coast Guard's decision. We will be ready to work when it does."

What a reopening usually looks like. Restrictions are lifted in stages, with draft limits or daylight-only transits first. With oil in the channel, operators should also expect conditions tied to the spill response.

Operator notes. Keep clear of the entrance and of response vessels working the bays. Confirm that agents have current positions and readiness. Do not plan on rumor. Gulfwater will report each change in port condition as it is issued.

stories.headline: Tankers return to Corpus Christi anchorage to wait as oil spreads across the bays
stories.dek: Ships that rode out Rafael at sea are back offshore. The channel stays closed while it is surveyed and the spill is contained, and sheen now covers about 33 square miles.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Tankers that put to sea ahead of Hurricane Rafael have returned to the offshore anchorage at Corpus Christi, where they are waiting for a ship channel that remains closed with no reopening date.

The Coast Guard says the channel will stay shut while it is surveyed and the Inner Harbor oil spill is contained. Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi, has declined to give a timetable.

The spill has grown as a factor since the storm passed. Surge and wind carried oil out of the ship channel into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, the Unified Command said. Sheen covers about 33 square miles, with oil on North Beach and Portland shorelines and in marshes. Cleanup crews began deploying boom as winds dropped.
"The ships are back. The port isn't," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "The market has stopped asking which day and started asking which week."
The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports, analysts say. Loadings have been halted since Sunday.

Holloway said the returning ships show that owners and charterers still expect to load at Corpus Christi and are not yet diverting in numbers. "Sitting at the anchorage is a bet that the wait is shorter than the alternative," she said. "That bet gets re-examined every morning."

She said crude that cannot load is accumulating in storage along the channel and at inland points that feed it. "Tanks are doing the work the ships would normally do. That works for a while," she said.
Two things would change the picture, she said: a Coast Guard statement on the channel survey, and a clearer account of how much oil is in the water near the docks.
Power outages across the area are also slowing the return of terminal staff and equipment checks.
No terminal has announced a restart date.

stories.headline: Week ahead: four conditions for a Corpus Christi restart, and none is met yet
stories.dek: A surveyed channel, a contained spill, working utilities and staffed terminals. The first full week after Rafael begins with exports still at zero.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The first full week after Hurricane Rafael begins with crude exports from Corpus Christi still halted and no date for a restart. Analysts say four conditions have to be met first.
A surveyed channel. The Coast Guard has kept the ship channel closed while it is surveyed. Ships that rode out the storm at sea are waiting at the offshore anchorage.

A contained spill. An estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released from two tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth. Oil has spread into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. On Saturday the state closed both bays to fishing and shellfish harvesting because of the oil.
Working utilities. The city issued a boil-water notice for all of Corpus Christi on Saturday, and power outages remain widespread. Terminals need power for pumps, lighting and safety systems.

People. Dock workers, line handlers, pilots, tug crews and terminal operators live in the same flooded and powerless neighborhoods as everyone else. A federal major disaster declaration for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties was approved Saturday.

"Any one of those can hold up the other three," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "The market is used to thinking about the channel. This time the channel is one item on a longer list."

Holloway said she was not attempting a restart forecast. "Anyone who gives you a date is guessing. What I can tell you is the order. Survey first, then the spill, because you cannot move ships through a response. Power and people run in parallel."

She said the fishing closure was a useful indicator for crude traders even though it has nothing to do with tankers. "It tells you the state thinks there is enough oil in that water to matter. The Coast Guard is looking at the same water," she said.
What to watch this week: any Coast Guard statement on the channel survey, the Unified Command's daily updates, and power restoration along the Inner Harbor.

stories.headline: Tanker systems vendor says its remote-access credentials were misused; Corpus Christi exports stay halted
stories.dek: Brightwake Marine Systems says it has revoked all remote access and is cooperating. Charterers are starting to ask which ships can be reached from shore.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — A company that maintains tanker cargo-control systems said Wednesday that its remote-maintenance credentials had been misused, two days after the Coast Guard said investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to the two tankers involved in the Corpus Christi oil spill.

"Our remote-maintenance credentials were misused," said Owen Pryce, chief executive of Brightwake Marine Systems. "We have revoked all remote access to customer vessels and we are cooperating with investigators. We do not know who did this."
Pryce did not say which vessels were affected. The Coast Guard has not named any vendor in connection with its investigation and has released no findings.

An estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived. The ship channel has been closed since the day before landfall and crude exports from the port, about half of the U.S. total, remain halted.
For the tanker market, the disclosure raises a question that reaches beyond Corpus Christi.

"Charterers vet ships for age, inspection history and crew. This adds a line," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Who can touch the cargo system, and from where? A week ago nobody was asking. Today some are."

Holloway said she had no information on how many vessels use remote maintenance of the kind Brightwake provides. She said shore-based support for shipboard systems is common across the industry because it saves sending technicians to a ship.

She said the immediate market effect is limited because Corpus Christi is not loading in any case. "The channel is the constraint. This is about what happens after, and whether terminals and charterers want assurances before a ship comes alongside," she said.
Rendal Terminals has said it is cooperating fully with the Unified Command.
No reopening date has been set for the channel.

stories.headline: Eleven days without Corpus Christi: how the U.S. crude export system is bending
stories.dek: Storage is filling, some buyers are looking at other Gulf ports, and ships are still waiting offshore. An analyst describes a system absorbing the gap rather than replacing it.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude exports from Corpus Christi have been halted for 11 days. The port normally handles about half of the U.S. total. Sabal asked how the rest of the system is coping.

"The system is bending. It is not rerouting," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics, which tracks Gulf Coast crude flows. "There is no second Corpus Christi to send it to."
Holloway described three ways the gap is being absorbed.
Storage. Crude that would have loaded is sitting in tanks along the ship channel and at points inland. "That is the first cushion and the biggest. It is also the one with a hard limit," she said.

Other ports. Some buyers are asking about loading at other Gulf Coast terminals. Holloway said those outlets were busy before the storm and can take some extra cargoes, not all of them. "You can move a few ships. You cannot move a port," she said.

Waiting. Ships that rode out Hurricane Rafael at sea are back at the offshore anchorage. Their owners and charterers are paying to wait. "Every ship still sitting there is somebody betting the restart comes before it is cheaper to leave," she said.
What she is not seeing, she said, is producers cutting output because of the halt. "That is the step after tanks fill. I would not rule it out if this runs long."

Two developments this week added uncertainty without changing the physical picture, Holloway said. The Coast Guard said investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of the tankers involved in the Inner Harbor spill. And a vendor said its remote-access credentials had been misused.
"Neither one opens or closes the channel," she said. "But they tell you the investigation is not a formality, and investigations take time."
The Coast Guard has given no reopening date.

stories.headline: Ten days shut: what has to be checked before Corpus Christi's channel can reopen
stories.dek: Depths, buoys, debris and oil. A working list of what stands between the offshore anchorage and the docks, and why nobody is offering a date.
body: Port condition, Corpus Christi, Friday: closed to all traffic for the 12th day. Ships that rode out Hurricane Rafael at sea remain at the offshore anchorage. No reopening date has been issued.
Gulfwater asked what has to be true before deep-draft ships move again. The working list:
Depths. A hurricane moves sediment. Rafael pushed about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays, and the dredged channel is the deepest water in a shallow system.

"A surge like that rearranges a shallow bay," said Dr. Nathan Brooks, a coastal oceanographer at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi who models storm surge. "I would not assume the bottom is where the chart says until someone has measured it."
Aids to navigation. Buoys can drag off station and range lights can be damaged. Pilots need them verified before taking a loaded tanker through the jetties.
Obstructions. Debris, sunken small craft and anything torn loose from shore have to be found and marked or removed.

Oil. This is the item that makes Corpus Christi different from an ordinary storm closure. Oil from the Inner Harbor spill was carried into both bays, and state agencies have closed fishing and shellfish harvesting there. Boom and response vessels are working in and near the channel, and ships cannot move through that work.

"Reopening comes in stages, and the survey sets the pace," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "The spill response is part of that picture. We will announce each stage when it is ready and not before."

What operators can do now. Keep ships at the anchorage ready to move on short notice. Expect draft or daylight limits on the first transits. Expect the order of arrivals to be set with the pilots, not by time at anchor alone. Ask terminals at the Inner Harbor what conditions they will set near the spill site.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi water plant on temporary pumps as utility waits for parts
stories.dek: The O.N. Stevens plant lost both power feeds in the storm. The utility says damaged pumps need replacement parts and capacity is limited, a constraint for a city trying to restart its industry.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Corpus Christi's main water treatment plant is running on temporary pumps while the utility waits for replacement parts, limiting capacity ten days after Hurricane Rafael, the city water utility said Friday.

The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant lost both of its power feeds early in the storm and its pumps were damaged. Water pressure fell across the city, and a citywide boil-water notice has been in effect since last Saturday.

"The damaged pumps need replacement parts, and the temporary pumps can only do so much," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokeswoman for the city water utility. "We are sorry. We know how hard this is. Please keep conserving and keep boiling your water until we tell you otherwise."
Gallegos did not give a date for the parts or for lifting the notice.

The plant's status matters beyond households. Corpus Christi's ship channel is lined with crude terminals and refineries, and the city's recovery is tied to the same utilities its residents depend on.

"When people ask me what has to happen before this port is back, they expect a list of channel items," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Water is on the list. It is not a crude number, but it is on the list."

Holloway said she had no information that water supply was the limiting factor for any terminal. The ship channel remains closed by the Coast Guard while it is surveyed and the Inner Harbor oil spill is contained, and that closure is what is keeping exports at zero.
"Right now nothing can load because nothing can sail," she said. "I am watching utilities because they decide how fast things move once the channel opens."
The utility said crews are working at the plant around the clock.
The Coast Guard has not set a reopening date for the channel. Crude exports have been halted since the port closed to inbound ships ahead of the storm.

stories.headline: Claims center opens for Corpus Christi spill as owners' liability takes shape
stories.dek: The center, run for the tankers' owners, takes cleanup and property damage claims as federal oil spill law requires. Who ultimately pays may depend on an investigation that has barely begun.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — A claims center run for the owners of the two tankers involved in the Corpus Christi oil spill opened Sunday for cleanup and property damage claims, as federal oil spill law requires.

The center will take claims from people and businesses with oil on their property or cleanup costs from the spill. An estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived.

"The claims center is open," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "If you have oil on your property or you paid to clean it up, document it. Photographs, receipts, dates. Then file."

Under federal law, the owners of a vessel that discharges oil are responsible in the first instance for cleanup costs and damages, and must show they have the financial means to pay. Gulfwater Maritime Report reported that the tanker owners posted financial assurance with the Coast Guard.
For the tanker and insurance markets, the larger question is what happens afterward.
"The law says who pays first. The investigation decides who pays last," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics.

The Coast Guard has said investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems. If a third party caused the release, Holloway said, owners and their insurers would be expected to seek recovery. "That is years of lawyers. It doesn't change who writes the first checks," she said.

Claims so far are limited to cleanup and property. The state has closed Nueces and Corpus Christi bays to fishing and shellfish harvesting because of the oil, and commercial fishers have asked when claims for lost income will be taken. Whitaker said he had no date.
The ship channel remains closed. Crude exports from the port have been halted for two weeks.

stories.headline: New boil-water notice for two Corpus Christi districts underlines utility strain
stories.dek: The city says low pressure in part of the system means contamination cannot be ruled out. About 48,000 residents are covered, on top of a citywide notice already in force.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The City of Corpus Christi issued a boil-water notice Sunday evening for Districts 3 and 4, saying low water pressure in part of the distribution system meant contamination could not be ruled out.
About 48,000 residents are covered, the city said. The notice comes on top of a citywide boil-water notice that has been in effect since Sept. 18.

The city attributed the low pressure to storm damage to treatment and pumping infrastructure. The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant lost both power feeds during Hurricane Rafael and has been running on temporary pumps while the utility waits for replacement parts.

"Pressure in that part of the system is lower than we can accept," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokeswoman for the city water utility. "When pressure drops, we cannot rule out contamination. This is a precaution, and it is a necessary one. Boil your water. We are sorry to be asking again."
Gallegos said the notice would stay in place until pressure recovers and tests come back clean.

For the energy sector, the notice is another reading on how far the city's utilities are from normal two weeks after landfall. The ship channel remains closed by the Coast Guard, and crude exports have been halted since the day before the storm. But terminals, refineries and the workers who run them rely on the same water and power systems.

Market participants said the notice does not change the outlook for exports, which depends on the channel. One terminal manager, who asked not to be named because he was not authorized to speak for his company, said his site had its own contingency arrangements for water. "It is our people I worry about," he said. "They go home to this."
Power has not been fully restored in parts of the city.
The utility has not said when replacement pump parts will arrive.

stories.headline: Federal authorities examining pre-storm drone flights over port and a utility site, sources say
stories.dek: Sources familiar with the investigation say commercial drones may have flown over the Port of Corpus Christi and at least one power utility facility in the week before Rafael. The FBI is asking for tips.
body: Federal authorities are examining whether commercial drones conducted surveillance flights over the Port of Corpus Christi and at least one local power utility facility in the days before Hurricane Rafael, sources familiar with the investigation told Gulfwater.
What the sources say. The flights took place in the week before landfall. They were detected through radar records maintained by the Coast Guard. No organization has claimed responsibility.

Why investigators care. The timing has drawn attention because of the damage to critical infrastructure during and after the storm, the sources said. They did not say that the flights caused any of it, and Gulfwater has no information that they did.

On the record. The Federal Aviation Administration and Customs and Border Protection's Air and Marine Operations confirmed Wednesday that investigators had identified multiple incidents of unauthorized unmanned aircraft operations in the Corpus Christi area in the period before the storm. The agencies said the aircraft flew without required authorizations and were detected through radar and electronic sensor records. They released no numbers, locations or times.

"We can confirm the FBI is investigating reports of unauthorized drone activity in the Corpus Christi area," said Mark Ellery, a spokesman for the FBI's Houston Division. "Anyone with information should contact the FBI. We have no further comment."
The Coast Guard declined to discuss the radar records.
Port condition. Unchanged. The ship channel remains closed to all traffic while it is surveyed and the Inner Harbor spill is contained.
Not known. Who operated the aircraft. How many flights there were. Which port and utility sites were overflown. Whether the flights are connected to any other matter under investigation.

Operator notes. Terminal security officers who logged drone sightings in early September should preserve camera footage and gate records and report them to the FBI. Gulfwater does not speculate on attribution and will report findings as agencies release them.

stories.headline: Report of pre-storm drone flights over port and utility site adds a security question for energy operators
stories.dek: Gulfwater Maritime Report says federal authorities are examining whether drones surveilled the Port of Corpus Christi and a power utility facility before Rafael. The FBI confirms only that it is investigating.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Federal authorities are examining whether commercial drones flew surveillance over the Port of Corpus Christi and at least one local power utility facility in the days before Hurricane Rafael, Gulfwater Maritime Report reported Thursday, citing sources familiar with the investigation.

The trade publication said the flights were detected through radar records maintained by the Coast Guard and took place in the week before landfall. No organization has claimed responsibility, it said.
Sabal has not independently confirmed the report.

"We can confirm the FBI is investigating reports of unauthorized drone activity in the Corpus Christi area," said Mark Ellery, a spokesman for the FBI's Houston Division. "We have no further comment." The FBI has asked the public for tips.

The Federal Aviation Administration and Customs and Border Protection said Wednesday that investigators had identified multiple incidents of unauthorized drone operations in the area in the period before the storm. They gave no locations.

For energy companies along the ship channel, the report lands in an already crowded security picture. The Coast Guard is examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of two tankers involved in the Inner Harbor oil spill.
No agency has said the drone flights are connected to the spill or to any storm damage, and the Gulfwater report did not say so.

A security manager at one area terminal, who asked not to be named because he was not authorized to speak publicly, said his company had been asked by federal investigators to preserve camera footage from early September. He declined to say more.

Terminals and refineries along the channel are subject to federal maritime security rules that require them to control access from land and water. Those rules were written with fences, gates and boats in mind.
The ship channel remains closed while it is surveyed and the spill is contained. Crude exports have been halted for nearly three weeks.

stories.headline: Explainer: what a closed ship channel means for Corpus Christi's refiners
stories.dek: Exporters with no ships have no sales. Refiners have pipelines, trucks and tanks, which buys time but not indefinitely.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Nearly three weeks into the closure of the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, most attention has gone to crude exports, which stopped the day the port closed to inbound ships. The refineries along the Inner Harbor face a different problem.
Sabal described in August how exporters and refiners share one channel. This is what the closure means for the second group.

What still works. Pipelines. Much of the crude that feeds the area's refineries arrives by pipeline from inland, and much of the fuel they make leaves by pipeline and truck. None of that depends on the ship channel.
What does not. Anything that moves by water. Feedstock that normally arrives by ship or barge, and products that leave by tanker, cannot move while the channel is closed.

"An exporter is a tap. A refinery is a machine," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "You can shut a tap. A machine wants to keep running, and it needs somewhere to put what it makes."

Holloway said she had no information on the operating status of any individual plant, and the companies have not made public statements. Hurricane Rafael also brought widespread power outages and damage across the area, which would affect any industrial site regardless of the channel.
In general, she said, a refinery cut off from the water leans on storage and on its land routes. "Tanks are time. When product tanks fill, you slow down. That is true for any refinery anywhere."

Why the market cares. Corpus Christi's refineries supply fuel to Texas and beyond. Holloway said a long closure would show up first in the trade of products that normally leave by ship. "The crude export gap is the big number. The products gap is smaller and closer to home," she said.
The Coast Guard has kept the channel closed while it is surveyed and the Inner Harbor oil spill is contained. Ships are waiting at the offshore anchorage. No reopening date has been set.

stories.headline: Week ahead: three clocks running in Corpus Christi, and the grid's is the newest
stories.dek: The channel survey, the spill response and now a power restoration that the utility says was set back by cascading substation failures.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Corpus Christi enters its fourth week without crude exports with three separate timelines in play. Two are familiar. The third became visible last week.
The channel. Closed by the Coast Guard while it is surveyed and the Inner Harbor oil spill is contained. Ships are waiting at the offshore anchorage. No date.
The spill. A claims center for the tankers' owners has opened. Fishing closures in the bays remain. The Coast Guard investigation into how oil left the two tankers continues.

The grid. Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority said Tuesday that restoration crews had encountered cascading substation failures in the northwest and central districts, extending the recovery beyond initial estimates. The utility said crews were at two facilities investigating protective relay conditions made worse by storm debris, and that it expected the final 32,000 affected customers to be restored within 7 to 10 days.

A federal aerial survey released Wednesday identified two CBPWA substations, Harbor View and Crosstown, as needing follow-up engineering inspection because of equipment configurations seen in the imagery.
"Two weeks ago I had the grid in the solved column. I have moved it back," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics.

Holloway said the areas named by the utility are not the ship channel itself, and she had no information that terminals lacked power. Her concern is pace. "A port restart needs people and services across the whole city. If a large part of town is still dark when the channel opens, the first week will be slower than the market assumes," she said.
The utility's 7-to-10-day window, counted from Tuesday, runs through the end of this week.
What to watch: CBPWA's restoration count, any finding from the substation inspections, and, as always, the Coast Guard.
"I would trade all three updates for one sentence from the Captain of the Port," Holloway said.

stories.headline: Texas energy operators told to review remote access after Corpus Christi utility intrusion
stories.dek: The governor has directed all critical infrastructure operators in the state to check remote-access procedures and report anomalies to CISA. Terminals and pipelines along the coast are on the list.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Energy companies across Texas are reviewing how outside parties connect to their control systems after the governor directed all critical infrastructure operators in the state to check remote-access security procedures and report anomalies to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

The directive followed confirmation Tuesday that the FBI and CISA are investigating unauthorized access to control systems at a Corpus Christi utility during the Hurricane Rafael response. Texas Cyber Command has been activated to assist. Officials have released no operational details and made no attribution.
Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority said Monday that it was investigating anomalous access to its internal network systems and that there was no indication customer data had been affected.

The order reaches well beyond one utility. Refineries, pipelines, crude terminals and power generators all count as critical infrastructure, and most allow some form of remote connection for vendors or their own engineers.

"The first step is a list," said Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with CISA. "Who can connect from outside, to what, and when did they last do it? Remove what is not needed. Separate control systems from everything else. If something looks wrong, report it. We would rather hear about ten things that turn out to be nothing."
Tran declined to discuss the utility investigation.

It is the second remote-access inquiry in Corpus Christi in three weeks. The Coast Guard is examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of two tankers involved in the Inner Harbor oil spill. No agency has linked the two matters.

Several operators contacted by Sabal declined to comment on their own reviews. A compliance officer at one pipeline company, who asked not to be named, said the instruction was clear enough. "Nobody needs to be told twice this month," she said.
The Corpus Christi Ship Channel remains closed and crude exports halted.

stories.headline: Slick containment removes one obstacle to a Corpus Christi restart; the channel decision remains
stories.dek: Unified Command says the main slick is contained and primary skimming is finished. The fishing closure has been extended, and the Coast Guard still has not set a date.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The main oil slick from the Corpus Christi Inner Harbor spill has been contained and primary skimming is finished, the Unified Command has said, removing one of the obstacles to reopening the ship channel.
The announcement does not reopen it. The Coast Guard has kept the channel closed while it is surveyed and the spill is contained, and has not set a date. Ships remain at the offshore anchorage.
"This is the first item to come off the list since the storm," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "It is not the last item."
The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports. Loadings have been halted for nearly four weeks.

The state has extended the closure of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays to fishing, a sign that officials still consider oil in the water a concern even as respiratory complaints near the shoreline ease.

"Containment is a milestone. It is not the finish," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "Shoreline work continues, and the fishing closure stays until the testing supports lifting it."

Holloway said the market should expect a staged reopening when it comes. "The Coast Guard does not usually go from closed to open. There are steps, with conditions. And any ship that has been through oiled water may need cleaning before it goes anywhere else," she said.
That last point could matter for the first weeks of loading, she said, because it would slow the turn of each ship at berths near the spill site.
Storage along the channel has absorbed the halt so far. Holloway said she continues to see no sign of producers reducing output because of it.
"What changed this week is that a restart moved from hypothetical to something people are scheduling around," she said. "Nobody has a date. But people have started asking terminals about slots."

stories.headline: When the channel opens, who moves first? Relief cargo, crude and a long line offshore
stories.dek: No date has been set. But the order of the first arrivals is already being argued, and a relief ship with 40 containers has been waiting since before the storm.
body: Port condition, Corpus Christi, Sunday: closed to all traffic. No reopening date issued.

The line. Ships that rode out Hurricane Rafael at sea have been waiting at the offshore anchorage since the week of landfall. Others have arrived since. When the Coast Guard reopens the channel, they cannot all move at once, and the first transits are likely to carry draft or daylight limits.
One ship in that line is MV Gulf Provider, carrying 40 relief containers booked before the storm by the freight forwarder Gulf Relief Logistics.

"I have forty boxes of relief supplies looking at the beach," said Terry Akins, the company's regional manager. "I understand the channel is closed for good reasons. I also know what is in those boxes and who is waiting for it. When there is a sequence, relief should be in front."

How sequencing works. The Captain of the Port sets the conditions. Within them, pilots, agents and terminals build the order. Time at anchor counts, but so do draft, berth readiness and cargo priority. A deep-laden tanker and a container ship do not need the same water or the same dock.

"We have a restart sequence drafted with the pilots, and it changes as the picture changes," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "Relief cargo is on the list near the top. The first day will be slow by design."

What has changed. The Unified Command has said the main slick from the Inner Harbor spill is contained and primary skimming is finished. The fishing closure in the bays has been extended. Containment removes one obstacle to navigation; it does not by itself reopen the channel.

Operator notes. Confirm draft, readiness and berth with agents now, so the ship can be slotted quickly. Expect conditions on transits near the spill site in the Inner Harbor. Expect the backlog to take days to work down after the first ship moves.

stories.headline: Week ahead: Corpus Christi begins a fifth week shut, with parts, audits and a survey outstanding
stories.dek: Pump parts for the water plant are shipping from out of state, a federal directive has operators auditing remote access, and the channel survey has no public end date.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Corpus Christi starts a fifth week without crude exports. The list of what stands between the port and a restart is shorter than it was, but three items are outstanding.

The channel. Still closed by the Coast Guard. The main oil slick has been contained, which removes one obstacle. The survey of the channel and the conditions for a first reopening have not been announced. Ships are waiting at the offshore anchorage.

The water plant. Replacement parts for the damaged pumps at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant are delayed. The utility said the supplier's local warehouse flooded and the parts are shipping from out of state. Temporary pumps continue to limit capacity, and boil-water notices remain.

The audits. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issued an emergency directive Thursday requiring federal agencies that run industrial control systems to audit remote-access credentials and configuration change logs within 72 hours. It strongly encouraged private owners of critical infrastructure to review the same. The directive followed a confirmed incident at a Texas utility.
"Every one of these has a version of the same answer," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "In progress, no date."
Holloway said the audits are unlikely to delay a restart directly. "Checking who can log in to your systems does not stop you loading a ship. Finding something might," she said.
She said the pump parts matter mostly as a measure of the city's general recovery. "A supplier whose own warehouse flooded is the whole story of this month in one sentence."
On the channel, she said traders have begun to plan around a staged reopening without knowing when it starts. "People are asking terminals about slots. Terminals are saying, ask the Coast Guard."
What to watch: any Coast Guard notice on port condition; the utility's restoration and repair updates; and whether more operators disclose findings from their access reviews.

stories.headline: Texas adds cyber emergency to Rafael disaster declaration; Corpus Christi utility running control systems by hand
stories.dek: The governor's amendment covers Corpus Christi utility infrastructure. FEMA has sent a cybersecurity rapid response team, and field crews are managing operations manually.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The governor of Texas amended the Hurricane Rafael disaster declaration Tuesday to add a cyber emergency component covering Corpus Christi utility infrastructure, the governor's office said.

The Federal Emergency Management Agency has deployed a cybersecurity rapid response team to assist local and state authorities. The affected utility has isolated its control systems as a precaution, and field crews are managing operations manually, the statement said.
The governor's office said the water supply remains safe when boiled and that electric restoration is continuing.

The amendment is the latest step in a sequence that began when the FBI and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency confirmed they were investigating unauthorized access to control systems at a Corpus Christi utility. CISA followed with an emergency directive on remote-access audits. No attribution has been made.
For energy markets, the practical question is whether a utility running by hand can support an industrial restart.
"I cover crude. This month I am reading utility notices, because the port does not restart on crude alone," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics.

Holloway said manual operation is slower and more labor-intensive but is something utilities train for. "Operators ran grids and water systems by hand for a century. It works. It does not scale well, and it leaves no margin if something else goes wrong," she said.

She said she had no information that the isolation had interrupted service to any terminal or refinery. The Corpus Christi Ship Channel remains closed by the Coast Guard for reasons unrelated to the utility, and crude exports have been halted for a month.
The declaration's wording matters for cost recovery, she said. Adding a cyber component can open federal assistance for response work that a storm declaration alone would not cover.
The utility has not said how long its control systems will remain isolated.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude loadings restart at reduced pace as inner-channel limits and backlog slow recovery
stories.dek: Two days into the partial reopening, ships are moving again. Spill decontamination still restricts the inner channel, and the line at the anchorage is weeks deep.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude loadings at Corpus Christi have restarted at a reduced pace two days after the ship channel partly reopened, with spill decontamination still restricting the inner channel and a backlog of ships waiting offshore.
The Coast Guard partly reopened the channel Thursday, a month after it closed ahead of Hurricane Rafael. The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports.

"Ships are moving. Not as many as we want, and not as fast," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "The inner channel is still under restrictions for decontamination, and we have a long line at the anchorage. We are working it one ship at a time."
