The backlog is delaying all kinds of cargo, including relief shipments that have been waiting since before the storm.
"Open is not the same as normal," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "The market got the first word this week. It is still waiting for the second."

Holloway said three things are holding the pace down. Transits are being sequenced carefully after a month with no deep-draft traffic. Berths in the restricted inner reach turn ships more slowly because of decontamination. And the queue offshore includes ships that have waited for weeks alongside new arrivals.

She would not estimate how long it would take to return to the pre-storm loading rate. "It depends on when the inner-channel restrictions come off. Until then you have a port working with one hand," she said.
Storage along the channel, which absorbed a month of crude that could not ship, will start to draw down as tankers load, she said. "That is the pressure valve opening. It does not open all at once."
Buyers who diverted to other Gulf ports during the closure are not expected to return immediately. "People who made other arrangements will finish them," Holloway said.
The Coast Guard has not said when the remaining restrictions will be lifted.

stories.headline: MV Gulf Provider berths and lands 40 relief containers, about a month late
stories.dek: The cargo was booked before Rafael and waited offshore through the closure and the backlog that followed the partial reopening. Inner-channel restrictions remain.
body: MV Gulf Provider berthed at Corpus Christi on Sunday and unloaded 40 relief containers, about a month after the cargo was meant to arrive.

The containers were booked before Hurricane Rafael by the freight forwarder Gulf Relief Logistics. The ship waited at the offshore anchorage through the storm closure, then waited again in the backlog that built when the channel partly reopened Thursday.

"Those boxes were booked five days before landfall. They touched the dock today," said Terry Akins, the company's regional manager. "Nobody on that ship did anything wrong. Nobody at the port did anything wrong. We had a plan that depended on one channel, and the channel was shut."
Port condition. Partly open. Spill decontamination continues to restrict the inner channel, which limits how many ships can work the Inner Harbor berths and slows the turn of those that do.

Why relief cargo waited after the reopening. A partial reopening does not clear an anchorage. Transits resumed under conditions, and the line offshore held weeks of arrivals. Sequencing put ships through by draft, berth and readiness as well as priority.

"Getting that ship alongside was a priority for us within the limits we are working under," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "The backlog is real and it is shrinking. Every day the channel stays open, the line gets shorter."

What was aboard. Akins described the cargo as general relief supplies consigned to agencies working in the three coastal counties. Trucks began moving containers off the terminal the same afternoon, he said.

Operator notes. Expect the backlog at the anchorage to persist while the inner channel stays restricted. Confirm decontamination requirements with the Coast Guard and the terminal before arrival. Ships bound for berths outside the restricted reach should say so early; it affects their place in the line.
Gulfwater first reported on the forwarder's standby contracts in August.

stories.headline: Port and utility to field drone-detection network across infrastructure corridor
stories.dek: The joint initiative follows a federal report on unauthorized drone flights before Rafael. The sensing network is expected to be working within 90 days.
body: The Port of Corpus Christi Authority and Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority will deploy a drone-detection network across the port and utility corridor, the two agencies announced Saturday.

What it is. A radio-frequency sensing and direction-finding network at multiple sites, operated in coordination with the Federal Aviation Administration and Customs and Border Protection's Air and Marine Operations. The agencies said Sentinel Airspace Inc. was selected as the technology provider after a competitive evaluation.
When. The network is expected to be operational within 90 days.

Why. The announcement cites a recommendation in the joint FAA and CBP report on unauthorized drone activity before Hurricane Rafael. The two federal agencies confirmed in late September that investigators had identified multiple unauthorized flights in the Corpus Christi area in the period before the storm. Gulfwater reported Sept. 30, citing sources familiar with the investigation, that authorities were examining whether drones had flown over the port and at least one power utility facility in the week before landfall.

"We would rather know what is flying over the docks than guess," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "This is a detection system. It tells us and our federal partners what is in the air and where it came from. We are not going to discuss where the sensors sit."
What it is not. The agencies described a network that detects and locates. They did not describe any capability to interfere with aircraft, which is tightly restricted under federal law.
Port condition. Partly open. Inner-channel restrictions for spill decontamination remain, and the anchorage backlog is still working down.

Operator notes. Terminals that fly their own drones for inspections or security should expect to be asked to register those flights once the network is running, so authorized aircraft can be told from unauthorized ones. Ship operators should remind crews that flying personal drones from vessels in port is not permitted without authorization.
The FBI investigation into the pre-storm flights remains open.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi utilities clear three hurdles in two days: power, control systems and pump parts
stories.dek: The last customers have power, the utility says its control-system cleanup has finished an initial phase, and replacement pump parts have reached the water plant.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Corpus Christi's utilities cleared three recovery milestones this week, five weeks after Hurricane Rafael.

Power. Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority said Tuesday that the final 3,200 customers in northwest Corpus Christi had been restored after relay inspection, repair and hardening work. All load zones are above 99 percent restoration, the utility said.

Control systems. CBPWA and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency said Wednesday that the utility had completed an initial phase of remediation after a confirmed security incident affecting its industrial control system network. Security monitoring has returned to normal status and no customer data was taken, they said. CISA issued an advisory to other infrastructure operators on the techniques observed.

Water. Replacement parts for the damaged pumps at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant arrived Wednesday. They had been delayed after the supplier's local warehouse flooded and the order had to ship from out of state.

"The parts are here," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokeswoman for the city water utility. "Now we install them and test, and the boil-water notice stays until the tests pass. We are close. Please stay with us a little longer."

The three updates matter to the energy sector because the port's restart depends on the city around it. The ship channel partly reopened last week, and crude loadings have resumed at a reduced pace while spill decontamination restricts the inner channel.

A terminal manager, who asked not to be named because he was not authorized to speak for his company, said the power restoration mattered most to his workforce. "My operators have been running a dock all day and going home to a generator," he said. "That ended this week for the last of them."
CBPWA said it is conducting a post-incident review and will add security measures identified in the investigation. Federal investigators have not attributed the intrusion.
The utility has not set a date for lifting the boil-water notice.

stories.headline: Week ahead: Corpus Christi waits on inner-channel limits as city services return
stories.dek: The citywide boil-water notice is lifted and power is back. On the water, decontamination still restricts the inner channel, and pilots in the air have reported GPS interference.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Ten days after the Corpus Christi Ship Channel partly reopened, the city around the port is closer to normal than the port itself.

City services. The citywide boil-water notice was lifted Saturday after pump repairs and testing at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant. Districts 3 and 4 remain under a separate notice. Power has been restored to the last customers.
The channel. Spill decontamination continues to restrict the inner channel. Crude loadings are running below the pre-storm pace and the backlog at the offshore anchorage is working down slowly.
"The city is nearly back. The port is half back," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "The half that is missing is the inner channel."

Holloway said the timing of that last step is the main variable for crude flows this week. The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports in normal operation. "When those restrictions lift, every berth turns ships at full speed again. Until then the anchorage empties slower than it fills," she said.

A new item. Pilots have reported GPS interference within about 40 miles of Corpus Christi, and the Federal Aviation Administration has issued a notice. Relief flights into the area are continuing on backup navigation.

The notice is addressed to aviation and no agency has reported any effect on shipping. Holloway said the market had not reacted. "It is on my list because it is unexplained and it is here. That is all I can say about it," she said.
Storage along the channel is drawing down as cargoes load. Holloway said some buyers who diverted to other Gulf ports during the closure have begun asking about Corpus Christi slots for November.

What to watch: a Coast Guard notice lifting the inner-channel restrictions; the Unified Command's status for the spill cleanup; the remaining boil-water notice; and any explanation of the interference.
"If the restrictions come off this week, the conversation in November is about volume again," Holloway said.

stories.headline: GPS interference near Corpus Christi: what the FAA notice says, and what it means on a ship's bridge
stories.dek: Pilots have reported interference within about 40 miles of the city. The notice is for aviators, but the habits that protect a flight deck are the same ones that protect a wheelhouse.
body: Pilots have reported GPS interference within about 40 miles of Corpus Christi, and the Federal Aviation Administration has issued a notice to aviators. Relief flights are continuing on backup navigation.

"Pilots operating near Corpus Christi have reported interference with GPS, and we have issued a notice so crews plan for it," said Lynn Carver, a regional spokesperson for the FAA. "Aircraft have other ways to navigate, and flights are continuing."
The notice is addressed to aviation. Gulfwater readers have asked what it means afloat. What follows is general seamanship, not a report of any incident on the water.

Why mariners should care. Satellite positioning feeds more than the chart display. On a modern bridge it also feeds the AIS transponder, the radar overlay and the clocks that other equipment relies on. When the input is wrong, several screens can be wrong together, and they will agree with each other.

What to do. Fix position by more than one method. In the approaches to Corpus Christi that means radar ranges and bearings, visual bearings on the jetties and ranges, and the depth sounder checked against the chart. Compare, and write the comparison down. Treat a sudden jump in position, speed or time as a warning, not a glitch.

"The Coast Guard expects mariners to fix their position by all available means, every watch, whether or not anyone has reported a problem," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. She declined to discuss the interference reports.
Pilotage. Ships transiting the channel carry a pilot who works largely by eye, radar and local knowledge. That is the strongest protection in confined water.
Port condition. Partly open; inner-channel restrictions for spill decontamination remain.

Operator notes. Brief bridge teams before arrival. Report suspected interference to the Coast Guard with time, position and what the equipment showed. Do not adjust equipment settings to make an alarm go away.

stories.headline: Last boil-water notice lifted in Corpus Christi; water plant back at full capacity
stories.dek: Districts 3 and 4 were the final areas under notice. The city says pressure and testing now meet state standards, closing out the utility's storm recovery.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The boil-water notice for Corpus Christi's Districts 3 and 4 was lifted Tuesday, ending the last water restriction in the city six weeks after Hurricane Rafael.

The city said water pressure across the affected zone had been confirmed above 40 psi at all test points and that water quality testing met state standards. The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant is operating at full capacity, it said.
"You can drink the water," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokeswoman for the city water utility. "Thank you for boiling it for as long as you did. We know what we asked of you."

The citywide notice was lifted Saturday after replacement pump parts were installed and tested. Districts 3 and 4, where low pressure had prompted a separate notice in late September, stayed under restriction until Tuesday.
The plant lost both power feeds early in the storm and ran for weeks on temporary pumps while replacement parts, delayed when the supplier's local warehouse flooded, shipped from out of state.

For industry along the ship channel, the announcement closes the utility chapter of the recovery. Power was fully restored last week, and Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority has said its control systems have returned to normal monitoring after a security incident that federal agencies are still investigating.

"That leaves the water the ships float in," said a shipping agent who asked not to be named because he was not authorized to speak for his principals. He was referring to the inner channel, where spill decontamination still restricts traffic.
The ship channel partly reopened Oct. 14. Crude loadings have resumed below the pre-storm pace.
Gallegos said residents who still see discolored water should run their taps for several minutes and call the utility if it does not clear.
The city has not yet said what permanent repairs or upgrades it plans at the plant. Gallegos said that review would come after the emergency work was complete.

stories.headline: Day two of the entrance closure: tug master describes blast off the port bow; cause still unknown
stories.dek: The harbor tug Corrin Bay is out of service and two of its crew are hurt. The Coast Guard has given no cause and no reopening time, and ships are holding on both sides of the jetties.
body: Port condition, Corpus Christi, Friday: ship channel closed to all traffic by Captain of the Port order. No reopening time issued.

What happened. An explosion went off beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties around 1 a.m. Thursday. The tug was damaged and two crew members were injured. The cause is unknown.

The master. "It came off the port bow," said Capt. Ray Dupree, 56, master of Corrin Bay, which is operated by Laguna Towing. Dupree has run tugs in the ship channel for 30 years. "First thing you do is count heads. I counted, and two of mine were hurt. Then you find out if the boat is going to stay under you. She did."
Dupree declined to guess at a cause. "I know what I felt. I don't know what it was," he said. "I'll let the people whose job that is tell me."

The Coast Guard. "The channel is closed by order of the Captain of the Port," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "The cause of the explosion is not known. We will not set a reopening time until we understand what happened and are satisfied the waterway is safe."

Timing. The closure came the same day spill cleanup moved to monitoring and the last inner-channel restrictions were lifted. On Thursday the port lost its last spill restriction and its only entrance within hours of each other.
Who is waiting. Loaded tankers inside. Inbound ships at the offshore anchorage. Military cargo: the Fort Hood aviation brigade's port movement, postponed in September, is delayed again.

Operator notes. All movements through the entrance are suspended, including small craft. Vessels inside should remain at their berths. Vessels offshore should hold at the anchorage and keep clear of the jetties and of Coast Guard units on scene. Report anything unusual seen near the entrance this week, with times, to the Coast Guard.
Gulfwater will report changes in port condition as they are issued.

stories.headline: FBI: GPS interference traced to transmitter in vehicle parked near Inner Harbor fuel terminal
stories.dek: The interference that pilots reported near Corpus Christi has stopped. Investigators found its source in an industrial area off the Inner Harbor, in a week when the ship channel is closed for another reason.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The FBI said Sunday that investigators had traced the GPS interference reported by pilots near Corpus Christi to a transmitter found in a parked vehicle in an industrial area near a fuel terminal off the Inner Harbor.

"Investigators traced the interference to a transmitter located in a parked vehicle," said Mark Ellery, a spokesman for the FBI's Houston Division. "The investigation is ongoing. We will not discuss evidence."
Ellery did not name the terminal or say who owned the vehicle.

Pilots had reported interference within about 40 miles of the city, and the Federal Aviation Administration issued a notice. "Those reports have stopped," said Lynn Carver, a regional spokesperson for the FAA.
The disclosure adds another unexplained security event to an energy corridor that has had several this fall.

The Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been closed since Thursday, when an explosion went off beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties. The Navy said Saturday that an explosive device caused it, and Navy teams are searching the channel with the Coast Guard. The FBI is investigating that as well. Crude exports are halted for the second time in two months.
No agency has said the interference and the explosion are connected. Ellery declined to answer when asked.

A security director at one area energy company, who asked not to be named, said firms along the Inner Harbor had been asked this weekend to review vehicles parked on or near their property. "You check your fence line every day. You don't usually check the street," he said.

Fuel terminals, like crude docks and refineries, are regulated for physical security at their gates and waterfronts. Radio interference from outside the fence is not something those plans typically address.
The FBI did not say when the vehicle was found.
Sabal will report further findings as they are released.

stories.headline: Analysts flag spoofed vessel identity near Corpus Christi entrance two weeks before blast; crude buyers ask what else is unknown
stories.dek: Officials decline to comment on any link. For the market, the question is no longer only when the channel reopens but what it would take to trust it.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Maritime analysts say a spoofed vessel identity appeared near the Corpus Christi entrance channel two weeks before the explosion that closed it, adding to the questions crude buyers are asking as the export halt enters its fifth day.

Public vessel-tracking data showed the identity of the fishing vessel FV Pelican Ridge broadcasting off Port Aransas overnight Oct. 14 to Oct. 15, while the same vessel reported a position about 600 nautical miles away. Analysts described that at the time as consistent with identity spoofing.

"I can tell you where the signal was. I cannot tell you what it means," said Ian McCready, an independent maritime security analyst and former Coast Guard watchstander. "It was near the entrance. That is a fact from public data. Anything past that is for investigators."
Officials declined to comment on any link to the blast.

The Navy has said an explosive device caused the explosion beside a harbor tug near the jetties Oct. 28. Navy teams are searching the channel with the Coast Guard, and the FBI is investigating. Crude exports from the port, about half of the U.S. total, are halted.

"After the storm the question was when," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Now there is a second question, which is whether. Whether the entrance is clear, and whether anyone can say so with confidence."

Holloway said that changes how buyers think about the closure. A storm closure ends when the weather and the survey allow. A security closure ends when authorities are satisfied, and that standard is harder to forecast.

She said she expected owners and insurers to ask more questions before sending ships back, though she had no information on any change in terms. "People will want to hear the Navy say the word clear," she said.
The Coast Guard has given no reopening date.

stories.headline: 'Count heads first': Corrin Bay's master and deckhand on the night at the jetties
stories.dek: Capt. Ray Dupree has not been back on the water. Deckhand Eddie Fontenot is recovering from a broken arm and a concussion. Both describe a routine job until it wasn't.
body: Capt. Ray Dupree has run tugs in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel for 30 years. Since the early hours of Oct. 28 he has not run one at all.

Dupree, 56, is master of the harbor tug Corrin Bay, operated by Laguna Towing. The tug was working near the Port Aransas jetties around 1 a.m. when an explosion went off off its port bow. The Navy has since said an explosive device caused it. The channel has been closed for a week.
"It was a regular job on a regular night," Dupree said. "Then the whole boat jumped. Count heads first. That is what you are taught and that is what I did."
Two of his crew were hurt. One was deckhand Eddie Fontenot, 29, who has a broken arm and a concussion.

Fontenot spoke by phone Tuesday. He kept his answers short. "I remember the noise. Then I was on the deck and my arm was wrong," he said. "Cap was there quick. Everybody was there quick. I'm grateful for that."
He said he does not remember much of the ride in.
Dupree has been visiting him most days. With Corrin Bay out of service, the captain has time. He said he does not like it. "A tug man with nothing to push is not good company," he said.

On the Navy's finding, Dupree chose his words. "Somebody put that there. I have been turning that over for a week," he said. "I am not going to say more than that, because I don't know more than that. The Navy and the FBI are working it. I will tell them anything they ask."

He said harbor crews have always watched the water at the jetties for logs, crab pots and small boats without lights. "You look for what can foul a wheel or hole a hull. Nobody trained us to look for this," he said.
Fontenot said he wants to go back to work. "I want to go back. Not this week," he said.

stories.headline: Two variables for crude: a crisis abroad and a closed channel at home
stories.dek: An overseas power has begun military operations, and its state broadcaster is mocking the Corpus Christi closure. An analyst says the market is pricing both and understands neither.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The crude market is working through two disruptions at once this week: a crisis abroad that escalated when an overseas power began military operations, and the continued closure of the U.S. port that handles about half of the country's crude exports.

The Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been closed for seven days, since an explosion beside a harbor tug near the entrance. The Navy has said an explosive device caused it and is searching the channel with the Coast Guard. No reopening date has been set.
"Either one alone is a story," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Together they are a week nobody wants to trade."

Holloway said the two events pull on the market in the same direction. A crisis abroad raises concern about supply from other regions. A closed Corpus Christi removes the largest outlet for U.S. crude that might otherwise fill a gap. "The barrels exist. They are in tanks in Texas. They cannot get to a ship," she said.

A foreign state broadcaster has mocked the port closure in its coverage, presenting it as a sign of American weakness. Holloway said traders should treat that as noise. "State television is not a market signal. The Coast Guard's notice is the market signal," she said.
U.S. officials have not connected the explosion to events abroad, and Sabal has no information that they are related.

What the market does not know is how long either disruption lasts. Holloway said that uncertainty, more than the lost volume so far, is what participants are reacting to. "A week of Corpus Christi is absorbable. We saw a month of it in September and October and the system bent without breaking. What is different is that nobody can describe the end of this one," she said.
Storage along the ship channel, drawn down since the October reopening, is filling again.
The FBI is investigating the explosion.

stories.headline: Second explosive device found near Corpus Christi entrance; crude export halt extends
stories.dek: Navy teams rendered the device safe. The find ends any expectation of a quick restart, on the ninth day of the closure.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Navy teams found a second explosive device near the entrance channel at Corpus Christi on Friday and rendered it safe, the Navy said, extending a crude export halt now in its ninth day.

"Navy explosive ordnance disposal personnel located a second device near the entrance channel and rendered it safe," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, public affairs officer for Navy Region Southeast. "The search continues. I will not describe the device."
The ship channel has been closed since an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties on Oct. 28. The Navy attributed that blast to an explosive device. The FBI is investigating.
The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports. No loadings have taken place since the closure.

"One device, you can tell yourself it was the only one," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Two, and the question becomes how many. That is a different kind of search and a different kind of wait."

Holloway said buyers who had held ships at the offshore anchorage in the hope of a short closure would now reconsider. "Yesterday you could argue for waiting. Today the people paying for those ships are going to ask for a plan," she said.

She said the find is not, by itself, bad news for the eventual restart. "You want them finding things. A search that finds nothing after one blast leaves people wondering. But it tells you the calendar is not days."
The Navy and Coast Guard have not said how much of the channel has been searched or how long the remaining work will take.

Storage along the channel is filling for the second time this fall. Unlike in September, terminals, power and city services are all working, and inner-channel spill restrictions were lifted last week. The only constraint on exports is the entrance.
The Coast Guard said the closure order remains in effect.

stories.headline: Explainer: what a Captain of the Port closure order does, and who it binds
stories.dek: The entrance at Port Aransas has been shut for 11 days. The order behind the closure applies to every vessel, and it ends only when the Coast Guard says so in writing.
body: Port condition, Corpus Christi, Sunday: entrance channel closed, day 11. No reopening date issued. Navy teams found a second explosive device near the entrance channel Friday and rendered it safe; the search continues.
Readers have asked what, in law, is keeping ships out. The short answer is an order from the Coast Guard Captain of the Port.

The authority. Federal law gives the Captain of the Port power to control vessel movement to protect a waterway, including by closing it or by setting a safety or security zone around a hazard. The order needs no vote and no hearing. It takes effect when issued.
Who it binds. Everyone. Tankers, tows, fishing boats, ferries and recreational craft. A zone around the jetties is as closed to a skiff as to a crude carrier.

"The order applies to every vessel, commercial or recreational," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "It ends by written notice from the Captain of the Port. We ask operators to wait for the notice and not to plan on what they hear on the radio or the dock."
How it ends. In this case, when the search of the channel is complete. The Navy is running that search with the Coast Guard.

"Our teams will continue until the search is complete," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, public affairs officer for Navy Region Southeast. "I am not going to describe methods or what was recovered. The standard is that the channel is safe for the ships that use it."

What a reopening notice usually contains. The time the order lifts. Any conditions on the first transits, such as daylight only or one-way traffic. Any zone that remains in force. Operators should read it for what it keeps as well as what it lifts.

Operator notes. Entering a closed zone can bring civil and criminal penalties. Agents should confirm they are on the Coast Guard's notice distribution. Crude exports remain halted until the entrance reopens.

stories.headline: Week ahead: Corpus Christi closure enters a second full week with the market asking who signs off
stories.dek: A storm closure ends with a survey. This one ends when the Navy and Coast Guard say the channel is clear, and owners and insurers will want that in writing.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been closed for 11 days. Navy teams found and made safe a second explosive device Friday, and the search of the channel continues. Crude exports are halted.
The question for the week is not only when the Coast Guard lifts its order but what owners, charterers and insurers will need to see before they act on it.

"The reopening notice is one document," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "The decision to send a ship is another, and somebody's underwriter is in that conversation."

Holloway said she had no information on any change in insurance terms for ships calling at Corpus Christi. Her point was about process. After a hurricane, a channel survey measures depths and checks buoys, and the industry knows how to read the result. After explosive devices, the assurance has to come from the Navy and the Coast Guard, and it rests on their judgment.
"That is not a criticism. It is the only way it can work. But the market is not used to it at a U.S. crude port," she said.

Ian McCready, an independent maritime security analyst and former Coast Guard watchstander, said outside data cannot shorten the wait. "There is nothing in a tracking feed that tells you a channel is clean. The people in the water tell you that," he said. McCready was among analysts who noted Monday that a spoofed vessel identity had appeared near the entrance two weeks before the blast. Officials have not commented on any link.
At the offshore anchorage, ships are still holding. Holloway said that reflects cost as much as confidence. "Leaving has a price too. A ship that sails for another port gives up its place here."
What to watch: any Navy statement on the progress of the search; any Coast Guard change in port condition; and whether ships begin leaving the anchorage in numbers.
The FBI investigation continues.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi export halt hits 13th day; port says restart plan is written and waiting
stories.dek: With spill restrictions gone and terminals staffed, the port says it can load as soon as the entrance opens. Storage is the clock the market is watching.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude exports from Corpus Christi remained halted Tuesday, the 13th day since an explosion near the Port Aransas jetties closed the ship channel. The port said it is ready to load as soon as the entrance reopens.
"Berths are clear and terminals are staffed," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "The plan for the first days is written. We need the entrance."
Navy and Coast Guard teams are still searching the channel after finding and making safe a second explosive device Friday. Neither service has given a completion date.

The situation differs from the storm closure in one respect that favors a faster recovery. Restrictions on the inner channel, imposed for decontamination after the September oil spill, were lifted the day the entrance closed. When ships can enter again, every berth will be available at full speed.

It differs in another respect that does not. "In September the tanks started with room," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "This time they started half recovered from the last closure. There is less cushion."

Holloway said she still had no evidence of producers cutting output because of the halt. She said that would be the next thing to watch if the closure ran well past two weeks. "Storage buys time. It has bought two weeks. I would not want to promise a month," she said.
The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports.

Some buyers have again turned to other Gulf Coast ports, as they did during the storm closure. Holloway said the pattern is becoming familiar. "The first time, people improvised. The second time, they had the phone numbers," she said. "Some of that business will be slower to come back."
Ships continue to hold at the offshore anchorage.
The Coast Guard said there was no change in port condition.

stories.headline: Beyond crude: general cargo and relief freight stuck again behind Corpus Christi closure
stories.dek: The forwarder whose relief containers waited a month offshore after Rafael says customers' cargo is held again. He is no longer planning around a single channel.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The closure of the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, now in its 14th day, is holding up more than crude.
Dry cargo, project freight and supplies bound for the hurricane recovery are waiting behind the same closed entrance as the tankers. For some shippers it is the second long delay in two months.
"I told my customers in October it would not happen twice," said Terry Akins, regional manager of Gulf Relief Logistics, a freight forwarder. "I have stopped saying that."

Akins's company booked 40 relief containers on the cargo ship MV Gulf Provider before Hurricane Rafael. The ship waited at the offshore anchorage through the storm closure and the backlog after the channel partly reopened, and berthed Oct. 17, about a month late.
He said customers' cargo is now held again. He would not say how much or for whom. "It is not forty boxes of water this time. It is the things people need to rebuild," he said.
The channel has been closed since an explosion near the Port Aransas jetties. Navy teams found and made safe a second explosive device last week and are still searching.
Akins said he does not question the closure. "Nobody wants a ship in there until the Navy says so. I want that more than anyone. My complaint is with my own plan," he said.

That plan is changing. Akins said he is moving some cargo by truck from other Gulf ports, at higher cost, and will write a second port into future contracts. "Corpus Christi is a good port. It has one door," he said.
Energy markets have focused on the crude export halt. The port handles a wide range of other cargo, and the same entrance serves all of it.
The Coast Guard has given no reopening date. Ships of all kinds continue to hold at the offshore anchorage.
Akins said he checks the Coast Guard's notices before he checks his email. "It is the only message that matters right now," he said.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi Ship Channel reopens after 14-day closure and full sweep
stories.dek: The Coast Guard lifts the closure order Thursday morning. Exports resume, and the first movements are sequenced with the pilots.
body: Port condition, Corpus Christi, Thursday morning: OPEN. The Coast Guard Captain of the Port has lifted the order that closed the ship channel on Oct. 28.
The 14-day closure ended after Navy and Coast Guard teams completed a full sweep of the channel. Crude exports are resuming.

"The Captain of the Port has lifted the closure order," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "The first movements are being sequenced with the pilots. Mariners should read the notice in full and follow the directions of the vessel traffic service."

The Navy. "The sweep of the channel is complete and the channel is clear," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, public affairs officer for Navy Region Southeast. She declined to add to earlier statements about what the teams found.

Background. An explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties closed the channel. The Navy said an explosive device caused it. Teams found a second device near the entrance channel on Nov. 5 and rendered it safe. The FBI is investigating.

The port. "Berths are clear and terminals are staffed," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "The plan for the first days was written while we waited. Today we work the plan."

What is different from October. When the channel partly reopened after Hurricane Rafael, spill decontamination kept the inner channel restricted and the backlog took days to move. Those restrictions were lifted Oct. 28. This restart has one constraint, the entrance, and it is now open.
Who moves. Loaded tankers held inside since the closure. Ships waiting at the offshore anchorage. Military sealift for the Fort Hood aviation brigade, whose port movement has been delayed twice.

Operator notes. Expect one-way sequencing and a slow first day. Confirm readiness with agents before requesting a pilot. Keep a sharp lookout at the entrance and report anything unusual to the Coast Guard.
Gulfwater will publish a first-day traffic report Friday.

stories.headline: First crude cargoes sail from Corpus Christi as channel works through its first full day open
stories.dek: Loaded tankers held inside for two weeks are leaving, ships are coming in from the anchorage, and military sealift is sharing the schedule.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Loaded crude tankers held inside the port for two weeks sailed from Corpus Christi on Friday, the first full day of operations since the ship channel reopened.
The Coast Guard lifted its closure order Thursday after a 14-day closure and a full sweep of the channel by Navy and Coast Guard teams.
"Tankers out, tankers in, and the Army's cargo loading," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "That is a good day."
The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports. Ships that waited at the offshore anchorage are being brought in under a sequence agreed with the pilots.

The channel is also carrying military cargo. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment, delayed twice this fall, began loading onto a sealift ship and will sail over the next five days.
"This restart is cleaner than October's," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "One constraint, and it is gone."

When the channel partly reopened after Hurricane Rafael, spill decontamination restricted the inner channel for two more weeks and the backlog cleared slowly. Those restrictions ended before the latest closure. Holloway said that should let loadings recover faster this time.

She said the first days would be dominated by ships already loaded or already waiting. New fixtures for Corpus Christi cargoes would follow as buyers regained confidence. "The physical recovery is quick. The commercial one takes longer. People who booked other ports will finish those voyages," she said.
Storage along the channel, which filled during the closure, is beginning to draw down.

Holloway said she expected questions about security at the entrance to continue. The FBI investigation into the explosive devices found there remains open. "The channel is open. The file is not closed," she said.
The Coast Guard said port condition is normal.

stories.headline: Regulators close emergency phase of Corpus Christi spill response after 60-day assessment
stories.dek: State and federal agencies say hydrocarbon levels in Corpus Christi Bay are back below the state standard. Long-term monitoring and the owners' claims process continue.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — State and federal environmental regulators have closed the emergency response phase of the Corpus Christi oil spill after a 60-day assessment found hydrocarbon levels in Corpus Christi Bay back below the state surface water standard.

The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality and the Environmental Protection Agency's regional office released the assessment Saturday. They said shoreline cleanup in Nueces Bay is nearly complete, with a short stretch near the Nueces Bay Causeway to be addressed in a spring maintenance program. Water quality at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant has remained within regulatory limits for more than seven weeks.
Long-term ecological monitoring of seagrass and oyster habitat in Nueces Bay will continue under a separate natural resource damage assessment, the agencies said.

"The emergency is over. The monitoring is not, and neither is the claims process," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program, which formed the Unified Command with the Coast Guard after the spill.

An estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released from two tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived. The spill kept part of the ship channel under restrictions until late October.
For the energy sector, the assessment formally ends the spill as an operating constraint on the port. The practical end came earlier, when inner-channel restrictions were lifted.
What remains is cost. A claims center run for the tankers' owners has been taking cleanup and property damage claims since September. Fishing closures in the bays are still in place.

And cause. The Coast Guard has said investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems. No findings have been released, and the question of who ultimately bears the cost of the spill depends on them.
The ship channel reopened Thursday after a separate two-week closure. Crude loadings have resumed.
Whitaker said residents who find tar balls should report them and should not handle them.

stories.headline: Spill claims center begins taking lost-income claims from fishers and shoreline businesses
stories.dek: The center run for the tankers' owners has handled cleanup and property claims since September. Claims left unpaid after 90 days can go to the Coast Guard's National Pollution Funds Center.
body: The claims center run for the owners of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay began taking lost-income claims Tuesday from commercial fishers and shoreline businesses affected by the Inner Harbor oil spill.
What changed. The center opened in September for cleanup costs and property damage, as federal oil spill law requires. It now also takes claims for income lost because of the spill.

Who may claim. People and businesses whose earnings fell because of the oil. In practice that means bay shrimpers, oystermen, guides, bait and tackle shops, marinas and waterfront businesses. Fishing and shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays have been closed by state agencies since four days after landfall.

The 90-day rule. A claim goes first to the party responsible for the spill. If it is denied, or is not settled within 90 days, the claimant can take it to the Coast Guard's National Pollution Funds Center.

"If the spill cost you income, file," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "Bring what you have: trip tickets, logbooks, tax returns, fuel receipts. The better the records, the faster it moves. The closures themselves are set by the state health and wildlife agencies, and they stay until testing says otherwise."
The spill. The Unified Command estimated about 9,000 barrels of crude were released from the two tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived.
"Rendal Terminals continues to cooperate fully with the Unified Command and investigators," said Victor Lang, a company spokesman. He referred questions about claims to the claims center.

For vessel operators. Ships that were delayed by the storm closure or by the inner-channel restrictions should take advice on whether their losses fall under the same law or under their charter parties. Those are different questions with different answers.
Not resolved. The Coast Guard's investigation into possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems remains open. Its outcome may bear on who ultimately pays.

stories.headline: Back on the tow wire: Corrin Bay's master returns to the channel on a borrowed boat
stories.dek: Capt. Ray Dupree went back to work this week, three weeks after the blast at the jetties. He says the job is the same. The way he looks at the water is not.
body: Capt. Ray Dupree went back to work this week on a boat that is not his.

Dupree, 56, is master of the harbor tug Corrin Bay, operated by Laguna Towing. Corrin Bay has been out of service since an explosion off its port bow near the Port Aransas jetties in the early hours of Oct. 28. The Navy said an explosive device caused it. The channel stayed closed for two weeks and reopened Nov. 11 after a full sweep.

The company has put Dupree on another of its tugs. He has run tugs in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel for 30 years, and he said the first assist felt like any other. "Line up, make fast, listen to the pilot, push when he says push," he said. "The work is the same. I look at the water differently."

He described the difference without drama. He slows his eyes down at the jetties. He asks the deck crew to call out anything floating, whatever it looks like. "We always watched for logs and pots. Now I want to hear about a plastic bag," he said.
Two of his crew were hurt that night. Deckhand Eddie Fontenot, 29, is recovering with his arm still in a cast. "He is mending and bored, which is the right order," Dupree said.
The channel he came back to is busy. Tankers held inside during the closure have sailed, the line at the offshore anchorage is working down, and military sealift moved through last week.

Dupree said harbor crews talk about the blast less than outsiders expect. "Tug men talk about the weather and the pilots and whose turn it is to cook," he said. "It is there, though. You see it when a boat comes in past the jetties and everybody on deck goes quiet for a minute."
He would not discuss the investigation. He said he expects Corrin Bay to work again.
"She took it and stayed up," he said. "I would like to be standing in her wheelhouse when she goes back out."

stories.headline: Two months on, Brightwake's remote access to tanker cargo systems remains switched off
stories.dek: The vendor revoked all remote connections in September after its credentials were misused. Its chief executive says technicians now attend ships in person and nothing reconnects until the rebuild is finished.
body: Brightwake Marine Systems has not restored remote access to any customer vessel, two months after it said its remote-maintenance credentials had been misused, chief executive Owen Pryce told Gulfwater.

Background. Brightwake maintains tanker cargo-control systems. On Sept. 20 the Coast Guard said investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, the tankers from which an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived. Two days later Brightwake said its credentials had been misused, revoked all remote access and said it was cooperating.
Status. Unchanged, Pryce said. "Every remote connection we had is off. Our technicians go to the ship. That is slower and more expensive, and slower and more expensive is acceptable," he said.

Pryce said the company is rebuilding how it connects to vessels before turning anything back on. He would not give a date. "I am not going to promise a month and then miss it. When it comes back, each session will have a named person on our side and a named person on the ship who agreed to it," he said.
He said the company still does not know who misused the credentials. "That is a question for the investigators. We have given them everything we have," he said.

The federal view. Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which is supporting the investigation, would not discuss the case. Her general advice to operators has not changed. "Know who can connect to your vessel, when they connect and why," she said. "And be able to cut that connection in minutes, not days."
Investigation. Open. No finding on the source of the access has been released.

Operator notes. Ask every vendor with shipboard access for a list of accounts and the date each was last used. Remove what is not needed. Require the master's or chief officer's consent before any remote session opens on a cargo system.

stories.headline: After two closures in one fall, a relief forwarder rewrites his hurricane playbook
stories.dek: Terry Akins's containers sat offshore for a month in September and October, and his customers' cargo was held again in November. His new plan starts from a different assumption.
body: Terry Akins keeps a binder he calls the playbook. This week he is taking pages out of it.

Akins is regional manager of Gulf Relief Logistics, the freight forwarder whose 40 relief containers on MV Gulf Provider waited at the offshore anchorage through Hurricane Rafael and its aftermath and came ashore Oct. 17, about a month late. In November his customers' cargo was held again when the channel closed for 14 days after the blast at the jetties.

"The old plan said: book the ship, book the berth, wait for the storm to pass," Akins said. "It assumed the channel would open in a few days. Twice this fall that was wrong, for two completely different reasons."

The new plan. Akins described three changes. Split the cargo, so that part moves by sea and part is staged inland within a day's trucking. Name a second port in the standby contract, with the right to divert before the ship joins a queue. And decide the diversion point in advance. "Once you are in the line at the anchorage, you have already lost the choice," he said.

The cost. More warehousing, more trucking and a contract that is harder to negotiate. Akins said the agencies he works for have not objected. "They remember where the boxes were on Oct. 4," he said. "They were looking at the beach."

The port's view. "We understand why customers plan alternatives, and we would in their place," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "Our job is to be reliable enough that the alternative stays in the binder."
Port condition. Open. The backlog from the November closure has worked down and waits at the anchorage are back to what operators call routine.
For other operators. The lesson is not specific to relief cargo. Any plan that treats a single entrance channel as a fixed point should say what happens when it is not.
Akins said the binder will be thinner. "Fewer pages. More phone numbers," he said.

stories.headline: Navy suspends emergency fuel supplier to Corpus Christi air station pending quality review
stories.dek: Quellmar Fuel Partners won a $2.1 million emergency contract after the storm. The review is linked to a backup generator failure at the station in October. The company says its fuel meets specifications.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The Navy has suspended Quellmar Fuel Partners, the emergency fuel supplier to Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, pending a fuel quality review linked to a backup generator failure at the station, the Navy said Sunday.
Quellmar was awarded a $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for the air station after the station's regular supplier flooded in Hurricane Rafael, federal contract records show.
The station's backup generator failed during a power interruption in late October. Power was restored and the cause was placed under review.

"The station has suspended deliveries from its emergency fuel supplier pending a fuel quality review," said Lt. Marcus Hale, public affairs officer for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. "There is no impact to operations."
Hale did not say what the review had found so far or how long it would take.

Quellmar disputed any suggestion that its product was at fault. "All product Quellmar delivered met specifications," said Nadia Kerr, the company's operations manager. "We are cooperating with the Navy's review and we expect it to confirm that."
A suspension is not a finding. It stops deliveries while the Navy tests fuel and examines records.

For fuel buyers, the case is a reminder of how emergency procurement works after a disaster. When a regular supplier is knocked out, agencies can award contracts quickly and without the usual competition. Speed is the purpose. It also means less time to check a new supplier's sources and handling.

Fuel quality reviews typically look at samples retained from each delivery, the paperwork that traces product back to a refinery or terminal, and the condition of the tanks it passed through. Water and sediment are the most common problems in stored diesel, and either can stop a generator.
The Navy has not said where it is obtaining fuel for the station's backup systems in the meantime.
Kerr said Quellmar would respond to any questions from the Navy. She declined to discuss the company's supply sources.

stories.headline: Explainer: how a Coast Guard casualty investigation runs, and when the public sees it
stories.dek: Readers ask every week when the tanker probe will report. There is no clock on it, and the reasons are built into how these investigations work.
body: Eleven weeks after about 9,000 barrels of crude were released from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth, the question Gulfwater hears most is when investigators will say how it happened. This explainer sets out how such an investigation runs.

Who investigates. The Coast Guard investigates marine casualties, including significant oil discharges from vessels. Here it has said federal cyber teams are assisting, because investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems.

What investigators collect. Statements from crew, terminal staff and vendors. Cargo and alarm records from the ships. Logs from shore systems. Physical evidence from valves and control equipment. Where computers are involved, copies of the systems themselves, which take time to examine.

Why it is slow. Evidence comes from several companies in several places, each with lawyers. Technical findings are checked before they are written down. And where a criminal question may exist, some material is held back so as not to prejudice it.

What has been said so far. On Sept. 20 the Coast Guard disclosed the remote-access line of inquiry. On Sept. 22 the vendor Brightwake Marine Systems said its remote-maintenance credentials had been misused and that it had revoked all remote access. Nothing further has been released.

"It will take the time it takes," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "Findings are released when the investigation is complete. We do not release them in installments, and we will not characterize an open investigation."

What the public eventually sees. A report of investigation, with findings of fact, conclusions and recommendations. Recommendations can lead to safety alerts or advisories for the whole industry before or after the report itself.

What operators should not do. Wait for the report before acting. The line of inquiry is public. Any operator whose cargo systems can be reached from shore already has enough information to review who holds that access.
Gulfwater will report findings when they are released and will not speculate before then.

stories.headline: Federal inspector general to review emergency fuel and debris contracts awarded after Rafael
stories.dek: The review covers contracts across the Coastal Bend, including the fuel deal now suspended by the Navy. Suppliers say they will cooperate.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — A federal inspector general has opened a review of emergency debris and fuel contracts awarded in the Coastal Bend after Hurricane Rafael.
The review was announced Tuesday. It did not name individual contracts.

Two have drawn public attention. Quellmar Fuel Partners holds a $2.1 million emergency contract to supply fuel to Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. The Navy suspended the company late last month pending a fuel quality review linked to a backup generator failure at the station. The company says its fuel meets specifications.

Separately, records show that Vantorra Restoration, which holds a county debris contract, billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's own surveys estimated. The company denies overbilling. The county has paused payments pending an audit.
"Quellmar will cooperate with the inspector general, as we are cooperating with the Navy," said Nadia Kerr, the company's operations manager. "We stand by our product."

Inspector general reviews of disaster contracts are common after large storms. They examine whether awards made under emergency rules followed the law, whether prices were reasonable and whether the government received what it paid for.

For energy suppliers, the fuel side of the review is the relevant part. Emergency fuel contracts are typically awarded within days, to whichever supplier can deliver, and often without competitive bids. Reviewers generally look at how a supplier was chosen, where its product came from and whether delivery records match invoices.
A review is not an accusation, and none of the companies has been charged with wrongdoing.

Suppliers that delivered fuel under emergency contracts in the region after the storm should expect requests for records, a procurement lawyer who asked not to be named told Sabal. "Keep everything. Bills of lading, test certificates, tank gauges. If you have it, the review is short," she said.
The inspector general's office gave no timetable.

stories.headline: Editor's notebook: your questions about the entrance channel, answered from the record
stories.dek: Is the channel safe? What was found? Is the vessel-identity anomaly connected? What is known, what is not, and what Gulfwater will not guess at.
body: Readers have sent more questions about the Port Aransas entrance than about any subject this year. These are the most common, answered only from what agencies have said on the record.
Is the channel open? Yes. It reopened Nov. 11 after a 14-day closure and a full sweep by Navy and Coast Guard teams. Port condition has been normal since.
What caused the explosion? The Navy said an explosive device caused the blast beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay on Oct. 28. Two crew members were injured.
Was anything else found? Yes. Navy teams found a second device near the entrance channel on Nov. 5 and rendered it safe.
Who put them there? Not known publicly. The FBI is investigating. No agency has named a person, group or motive, and Gulfwater does not speculate on attribution.
What were the devices? The Navy has declined to describe them. We have not asked sources to, and would not publish it.

Is the vessel-identity anomaly connected? In mid-October, public AIS data showed the identity of the fishing vessel FV Pelican Ridge broadcasting off Port Aransas while the same vessel reported a position about 600 nautical miles away. Analysts later noted the signal appeared near the entrance channel two weeks before the blast. Officials have declined to comment on any link.

"The timing is a fact. A link is a claim," said Ian McCready, an independent maritime security analyst and former Coast Guard watchstander. "I have the first and not the second. Public data cannot tell you who was transmitting."
Has anything changed for ships? No new standing restrictions have been announced for the entrance. Operators report closer lookout at the jetties, which costs nothing.

What should crews report? Anything unusual on or near the water at the entrance: unlit small craft, objects that do not drift like debris, divers where none are expected. Report to the Coast Guard with time and position.
What we do not know. The source of the devices, whether more will be said about them, and when the FBI will report.

stories.headline: Navy orders security review at Texas air stations, citing drone reports and the channel attack
stories.dek: The review covers Navy installations, not the port. The Coast Guard says port condition is unchanged, and the Navy is not discussing scope.
body: The Navy on Sunday ordered a security review at its air stations in Texas, citing the drone reports that followed Hurricane Rafael and the attack in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel.

"The Navy has directed a security review at its Texas air stations," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, public affairs officer for Navy Region Southeast. "The review takes account of the reports of drone activity and of the attack in the ship channel. I will not discuss its scope or its timeline."
What it covers. Navy installations. In this area that means Naval Air Station Corpus Christi and Naval Air Station Kingsville.
What it does not cover. The commercial port. The ship channel and its terminals fall under the Coast Guard Captain of the Port, the port authority and the terminal operators.
"The Navy's review does not change port conditions at Corpus Christi," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "The channel is open."

Why maritime readers should note it anyway. The review is the first time a federal agency has publicly placed the drone reports and the channel devices in the same sentence. The Navy did not say the two are connected, and neither does Gulfwater. But an installation that sits on the same bay as the channel is now looking at both.

Related. The port and Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority announced a drone-detection network for the port and utility corridor in October, expected to be working within 90 days of that announcement.

Open files. The FBI is investigating the explosive devices found at the entrance channel. The Coast Guard investigation into possible unauthorized remote access to two tankers' cargo-control systems remains open. Neither has produced public findings.

Operator notes. No action is required of vessel operators as a result of the Navy's order. Terminals adjoining Navy property should expect to hear from their neighbors. Continue to report unauthorized drone flights and anything unusual on the water to the Coast Guard.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi ends the year loading normally; buyers keep the backup plans they wrote this fall
stories.dek: The channel has been open six weeks and the anchorage is back to routine waits. What has not returned, an analyst says, is the assumption that the port is always there.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude is loading normally at Corpus Christi in the last full week of the year, six weeks after the ship channel reopened from the second of two closures this fall.
Tankers are again waiting at the offshore anchorage, which before September was a sign of a busy port and is being read that way again.
"The volume came back. The assumption did not," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Every buyer I talk to has a second port written down now."

The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports. It was shut for a month after Hurricane Rafael, with spill restrictions lasting two weeks longer, and for 14 days in November after explosive devices were found at the entrance.

Holloway said the lasting effect is in contracts, not flows. Buyers are asking for the right to load elsewhere if Corpus Christi closes, and for clearer terms on who pays when a ship waits. "Those clauses existed. People used to skip the page," she said.
She said sellers have largely agreed, because the alternative is losing the buyer. "Flexibility has a cost, and for now the seller is carrying some of it."

The port said it understands the caution. "We are closing the year with our customers shipping," said Javier Salinas, a spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "We will spend next year earning the word reliable back."

Three matters from the fall remain unresolved and could bear on that. The Coast Guard has not released findings on possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo systems of two tankers involved in the September spill. The FBI is still investigating the devices at the entrance. And no agency has explained a spoofed vessel identity seen near the channel in October.
"None of those stops a cargo today," Holloway said. "All of them are why the second port is written down."
Loadings are expected to continue through the holidays.

stories.headline: FBI searches offices of Navy's suspended fuel supplier and a storm debris hauler
stories.dek: Agents executed warrants at Quellmar Fuel Partners and Vantorra Restoration. Neither company has been charged. Quellmar says its fuel met specifications.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — FBI agents executed search warrants Monday at the offices of Quellmar Fuel Partners, the emergency fuel supplier suspended by the Navy last month, and Vantorra Restoration, a debris hauler hired by Nueces County after Hurricane Rafael.

"I can confirm that agents executed search warrants at both locations today," said Mark Ellery, a spokesman for the FBI's Houston Division. "I will not comment on what was sought or on the investigation."
Neither company has been charged with a crime. A search warrant requires a judge's approval and allows agents to look for evidence. It is not an accusation.

Quellmar holds a $2.1 million emergency contract to supply fuel to Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, awarded after the station's regular supplier flooded. The Navy suspended the company in late November pending a fuel quality review linked to a failure of the station's backup generator.
In a written statement, Quellmar said its product met specifications and that it is cooperating with authorities. Operations manager Nadia Kerr did not respond to a request for an interview.

Emergency debris and fuel contracts in the Coastal Bend have been under review by a federal inspector general since early December. Officials have not said whether the searches are connected to that review.
For the fuel trade, the searches raise the stakes of what began as a quality dispute. A suspension pending tests is a commercial matter. Search warrants are not.

A fuel distributor in South Texas, who asked not to be named, said customers had begun asking his company for documents they had not requested before. "They want the paper trail back to the rack," he said, using the industry term for the terminal where trucks load. "After this, I expect every emergency contract to ask for it up front."
The Navy has not released results of its fuel quality review.
Sabal will update this report if the companies respond further.

stories.headline: Maritime cyber advisory hands charterers a new vetting question for tankers
stories.dek: The Coast Guard and CISA want vessel operators to review who can reach cargo systems remotely. Buyers lifting crude are deciding whether to ask for proof.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — A joint advisory from the Coast Guard and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency urging vessel operators to review vendor remote access to cargo systems is prompting crude buyers to consider adding the question to how they vet tankers.

The advisory was issued Tuesday. It follows more than three months of investigation into possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of two tankers at Corpus Christi, from which an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released as Hurricane Rafael arrived.

"We are asking operators to know who holds a key to the cargo system and to be able to take it back," said Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with CISA. "Review vendor access. Keep cargo control separate from other networks. Log every session."
Tran declined to discuss the investigation.
The advisory does not impose new rules. Its commercial effect may come through charterers, who decide which ships they are willing to hire.

"An advisory is voluntary. A charterer's questionnaire is not," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "If the big buyers start asking for evidence of an access review before they fix a ship, every owner will have one within a month."

Holloway said she knew of no buyer that had formally changed its vetting requirements. She said several were discussing it. Terminals are having a parallel conversation, she said, about what they should know regarding a ship's systems before it connects to a loading arm.

The vendor at the center of the Corpus Christi case, Brightwake Marine Systems, said in September that its remote-maintenance access had been misused and that it had shut off all remote connections to customer vessels.

Holloway said the cost of compliance is small against the cost of a spill. "This is paperwork and a few difficult phone calls. Owners will do it. The question is whether they do it before the next charterer asks or after."
The Coast Guard has not released findings from its investigation.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi 2028: six items on the operator's watch list
stories.dek: The channel is open and the anchorage is routine. What carries over from 2027 is a set of unfinished reviews, and the next hurricane season is five months out.
body: Status, Corpus Christi Ship Channel, New Year's Day: open to all traffic. Waits at the offshore anchorage are routine. For operators planning the year, six items carry over.

1. Vendor access reviews. The Coast Guard and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issued a joint maritime cyber advisory Dec. 28 urging vessel operators to review vendor remote access to cargo systems. "An advisory is only useful if somebody opens the access list and reads it," said Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with CISA. "Start with who can connect, and remove what you cannot explain."

2. The tanker investigation. The Coast Guard has not released findings on possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay. Expect recommendations whenever it reports.
3. The entrance. The FBI investigation into the explosive devices at the Port Aransas entrance is open. No standing restrictions have been announced since the channel reopened in November.

4. Vessel identity. October's AIS anomaly off Port Aransas has no public explanation. "If you see a ship in two places, write it down and send it in," said Ian McCready, an independent maritime security analyst and former Coast Guard watchstander. "Patterns come from many small reports."

5. Drone detection. The port and utility's detection network, announced in October, was expected within 90 days. The Navy's security review at its Texas air stations, ordered in December, is running alongside.

6. Spill claims. The owners' claims center has taken lost-income claims since November. Claims unpaid after 90 days can go to the Coast Guard's National Pollution Funds Center, so the first of those dates falls in the coming weeks.

And one that never leaves the list: hurricane season opens in five months. The 2027 lessons are specific. Build timelines from X-Ray. Decide early about ships that stay alongside. Do not treat one entrance channel as a fixed point.
Gulfwater will track each item through the year.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi plans to harden power feeds to water plant that failed in Rafael
stories.dek: The O.N. Stevens plant lost both of its feeds early in the storm, setting off five weeks of boil-water notices. The city says the fix starts with the electricity.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The City of Corpus Christi plans to harden the power feeds to the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, the facility whose failure during Hurricane Rafael left the city under boil-water notices for five weeks, the city water utility said.
The plant lost both of its power feeds early in the storm. Its pumps were damaged, pressure fell across the system and the utility ran on temporary pumps until replacement parts arrived in October.
"The pumps were damaged because the power failed first," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokeswoman for the city water utility. "We are starting where the failure started."
Gallegos did not give a cost or a schedule. She said details would go to the city council.

For utilities and the industries that depend on them, the plan addresses a weakness that Rafael exposed plainly. A treatment plant with two power feeds is designed so that one can fail. At O.N. Stevens, both did.

Hardening can take several forms, engineers say: strengthening or burying lines, routing the two feeds so that a single event cannot take out both, and adding on-site generation large enough to run the main pumps. Each costs more than the last.
The announcement comes as the state reviews separate storm procedures, including when bridges close in high winds.

Energy companies along the ship channel will watch the outcome. Terminals and refineries have their own arrangements for water and power, but their workers and the city's services do not. During the recovery, analysts repeatedly pointed to utilities as a limit on how fast the port could restart once the channel opened.

A plant operations consultant, who asked not to be named because she has worked for the city, said the lesson reaches beyond water. "Everybody had two feeds on paper. The storm asked whether they were really two," she said.
The utility's separate review of its control-system security, begun after a federal investigation into unauthorized access, is continuing.

stories.headline: Federal filing: Navy's suspended fuel supplier and storm debris hauler share an offshore owner
stories.dek: A civil forfeiture filing says Quellmar Fuel Partners and Vantorra Restoration are owned by Brannoch Maritime Holdings and that accounts tied to them received about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Quellmar Fuel Partners, the emergency fuel supplier suspended by the Navy, and Vantorra Restoration, a storm debris hauler, share an owner, an offshore company called Brannoch Maritime Holdings, according to a federal civil forfeiture filing made public Thursday.
The filing lists Brannoch's director as L. Marrick. It says bank accounts tied to the two firms received about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid. It does not say how the aid was diverted.
A civil forfeiture case is brought against money or property, not against a person. Its claims are allegations that have not been proven in court, and no one has been criminally charged.
"All product Quellmar delivered met specifications," Nadia Kerr, the company's operations manager, said in a statement. "The company will respond in court."
Vantorra said it would respond through its attorneys.

Quellmar holds a $2.1 million emergency contract to supply fuel to Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. The Navy suspended it in November pending a fuel quality review. FBI agents searched the offices of both companies on Dec. 27.

For the fuel trade, the filing shifts attention from product quality to ownership. Emergency fuel contracts are awarded on a supplier's ability to deliver within days. Who stands behind the supplier is seldom examined at that speed.

A compliance adviser to fuel distributors, who asked not to be named, said he expected government buyers to tighten disclosure rules. "Ownership questions are normal in a competitive bid. In an emergency award they get skipped," he said. "I would expect that to change, and I would expect suppliers with complicated ownership to be asked to simplify it or sit out."
The filing does not allege that the fuel supplied to the air station was defective. The Navy has not released the results of its fuel quality review.
A federal inspector general's review of emergency fuel and debris contracts in the Coastal Bend, opened in December, is continuing.

stories.headline: Inner Harbor spill: about 4,200 damage claims filed as bay fishing grounds partly reopen
stories.dek: State agencies reopened part of the closed waters after testing. The claims count gives the first public measure of the spill's commercial reach.
body: About 4,200 spill damage claims have been filed over the Inner Harbor oil spill, and part of the fishing grounds closed since September have reopened after testing, officials said Friday.

The count. It is the first public figure for the spill's commercial reach. The claims center run for the owners of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay has taken cleanup and property claims since late September and lost-income claims since mid-November.

The water. Fishing and shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays were closed four days after Hurricane Rafael made landfall. Part of those grounds are now open. The rest stay closed pending results.

"The agencies reopened what the testing supports, and nothing more," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "Check the current closure maps before you leave the dock. If you have a claim, keep your records in order."

The 90-day mark. Under federal oil spill law, a claim that is denied or not settled within 90 days can be taken to the Coast Guard's National Pollution Funds Center. For the earliest lost-income claims, that date arrives next month.
The terminal. "Rendal Terminals continues to cooperate fully," said Victor Lang, a company spokesman. He declined to comment on claims or on the investigation.
